content:
A free trial Quran class is a short, free, one-on-one lesson, usually 25 to 30 minutes, where your child meets the teacher, reads a little, and you watch how the teaching feels. It costs nothing, it asks for no card details, and it commits you to nothing. If you are a parent in the UK, the USA, Canada, or Australia wondering whether online Quran classes will work for your child, this is the simplest way to find out.

Before anything else, remember the words Allah taught us to say when we seek knowledge:

وَقُل رَّبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا

"And say, My Lord, increase me in knowledge." (Surah Taha, 20:114)

A trial class is a small act of seeking knowledge. You are not signing up for a year of lessons. You are taking one careful step, and seeing where it leads.

What a Free Trial Class Actually Is

A free trial is a short introductory lesson between your child and a Quran teacher over a video call. Ours is genuinely free. No card details, no lock in, no pressure to continue. The word trial sometimes makes parents nervous, as if their child is being tested for admission. In my experience, the testing runs the other way. You are the one doing the evaluating.

The trial does three things. First, the teacher finds out where your child stands right now, whether that is Noorani Qaida, nazra reading, tajweed, or hifz. Second, your child discovers what learning the Quran through a screen actually feels like. Third, you get to watch the teacher at work: their patience, their manner, their way with children. That is hard to judge from a website. It takes one live lesson.

One warning sign is worth naming. If the trial feels like a sales call, with more talk about packages than about your child, believe what you just saw. A confident teacher lets the teaching speak for itself.

What Happens During the Trial: Step by Step

Every teacher has their own style, but a good trial follows a steady rhythm. Knowing it in advance helps your child relax, and helps you notice what matters.

1. A Warm Welcome and Introduction

The first few minutes are about comfort, not curriculum. I greet the child by name, ask about their age and school and what they enjoy, and let the conversation flow. A teacher who can make a shy seven year old smile in the first three minutes has a skill no certificate can measure. Watch your child here. Ease and laughter are good signs. Visible discomfort is information too, and you should trust it.

2. A Gentle Level Assessment

Next comes a quiet check of where your child stands. I might ask them to read a few Arabic letters, or recite a short surah they already know, or simply watch how they hold the mushaf. There are no wrong answers in this part. None. I am listening for pronunciation, fluency, and confidence, so I can suggest the right starting point, whether that is the Qaida or the nazra, hifz, or tajweed track. And if your child knows nothing yet, that is a perfectly fine result. Complete beginner is the most common starting level I see.

3. A Mini Lesson

This is the heart of the trial, around ten to fifteen minutes of real teaching. I pick one small, achievable piece of learning. A few letters with their makharij, the points of pronunciation. A short verse repeated together. A gentle correction to something your child already recites. Pay attention to the teaching style. Does the teacher break things into small steps? Do they praise effort? Do they correct without making the child feel small? These ten minutes are the truest preview you will get of regular classes.

4. Questions and Next Steps

The trial usually closes with time for your questions. Class timings, the course I recommend and why, how progress is tracked, what the fee is. A good teacher answers plainly and gives you space to think. Heavy pressure to pay on the spot is a red flag. You should leave the call knowing exactly what course fits your child, which time slots are open, and what it costs. With zero obligation.

How to Prepare Your Child

A little preparation turns a good trial into a great one. None of it needs special equipment, only a bit of intention.

Set up the tech the day before. Test the camera, microphone, and speakers on the device your child will use, and check the internet in the room where the class will happen. Join the video link five minutes early. Nothing deflates a child like spending the first ten minutes saying, "Can you hear me?"

Create a calm, clean space. A quiet corner with a small table works beautifully, the same setup I recommend in our parents' guide to online Quran classes. Switch off the TV, put the toys aside, and let the other children know the room is off limits for half an hour. If it is easy, face the qiblah. It gives the lesson a sense of occasion.

Do wudu together. Even on a screen, wudu tells a child this is sacred time, not screen time. It settles them. Keep the mushaf or Qaida nearby, on a rehal or a clean surface, within reach. If you do not have one at home, do not worry. I will share my screen.

Talk about it positively, and keep it light. Something like, "Tomorrow you will meet a Quran teacher on the computer. They will chat with you and teach you something small. There is nothing to be nervous about." Avoid phrases like "be on your best behaviour" or "answer correctly." Those words create exactly the anxiety you are trying to prevent.

How to Prepare Yourself as a Parent

Your job during the trial is to observe. Sit nearby, in view or just off camera, whichever the teacher prefers, and watch for the things that actually predict good learning.

First, does the teacher connect with your child? Patience, warmth, and the ability to hold a child's attention through a screen matter more than any credential. If you want a fuller picture of what to look for in a Quran teacher, that guide goes deeper.

Second, is the lesson structured? Even 25 minutes should have a beginning, a middle, and an end. Structure means there is a real curriculum behind the teacher, not random reading.

Third, how is correction handled? Every child will mispronounce things. The question is whether the teacher corrects with encouragement, like "good try, now watch my mouth," or with impatience. Your child will hear hundreds of corrections over the coming months. Make sure the tone is one you want them hearing every day.

Finally, prepare your questions in advance. Ask about experience with your child's age group, the exact course recommended and why, class length and how many times a week, how memorization and revision are handled, how you receive progress updates, and the fee structure, including any discount for siblings. Write them down. You will forget half of them in the moment otherwise.

After the Trial: Making the Decision

Sleep on it. A good decision the next morning beats a rushed one on the call. Ask your child how they felt. Children are remarkably honest about whether they liked a teacher.

Then look at the practical side. Do the offered time slots actually fit your family's routine in your timezone? Is the monthly fee something you can sustain for a year, not just an exciting first month? Be honest about fit as well. The kindest teacher in the world might still not be the right one for your child. Perhaps your teenager needs a firmer hand, or your younger child needs more play in the lesson. A good teacher will tell you honestly if a different approach would suit your child better. That honesty is itself a green flag.

One more thing the trial cannot show you: consistency over months, how revision is enforced, and what happens when motivation dips, as it always does at some point. Ask about those directly. The answers reveal a teacher's true character.

Start With Confidence

A free trial class is a small step with outsized value. Thirty minutes that can set the direction of your child's whole Quran journey. Prepare the space, prepare your child gently, observe with open eyes, and trust what you see. The right teacher will make your child feel capable, make you feel informed, and make the Quran feel close, even through a screen.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027)

That is what a trial class really is. A first step toward being among the best of people, for your child and for you. If you are ready, book a free trial class and experience it for yourself. And if you are still exploring, our guide on how online 1-on-1 Quran classes work answers the practical questions families ask most.

Is the trial class really free, and what happens after it?

Yes, the trial is genuinely free, with no card details and no obligation. If you decide to continue, you get a free 3-day trial of regular classes first, and only then does the monthly fee begin.

Who will teach my child?

I teach every class myself. I am M Muddasir Hameed, the founder of Noor E Quran Institute, and there is no other teacher. Your child meets the same teacher in the trial and in every lesson after it.

How much do the classes cost each month?

The monthly fee depends on how many classes your child takes each week, and the exact amount is confirmed during the trial, in plain words, with no hidden charges. Sibling discounts are available, so ask about them when you book.

Is it comfortable and private for my daughter?

Yes. Lessons are private, one-on-one video calls, and I keep them respectful and comfortable for sisters of every age. You are welcome to sit nearby during the trial and during regular classes, and I teach girls and women with the same care and privacy I would want for my own family.

title: Noorani Qaida for Kids: Start Your Child's Quran Journey
metaDescription: Discover why Noorani Qaida for kids is the essential first step in Quran learning: what children learn, best age to start, and how online Qaida classes work.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
A small book. Thin pages. Letters, over and over, until they feel like old friends. That is how every confident reciter started, whether they admit it or not. The book is the Noorani Qaida. And if you are wondering where your child should begin their Quran journey, well, this is the answer. Right here. Not with long surahs. Not with complicated rules. With letters, learnt well.

Let me explain what the Qaida is, why it matters so much, what your child will go through inside it, when to start, and what our online lessons look like day to day. No jargon. Just the honest picture, as I see it after years of teaching children one on one.

So, What Is the Noorani Qaida?

It is a primer. A first book. Its job is simple: teach a child the Arabic letters and how to read them. That is all it does, and it does it better than anything else I know. Children usually finish it within a few months. It is slim, yes, but do not be fooled by that. What your child learns in those few months will carry every single thing they read afterwards.

Molvi Noor Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, compiled it more than a century ago. Since then, madrasas, mosques and ordinary homes across the Muslim world have used it. Why has it lasted so long? Because it understands children. One small step. Practise it. Own it. Then the next step. It never piles five new things on a child at once, and that patience is exactly what young learners need.

Think about phonics, if your child attends school in the UK, the US, Canada or Australia. Children learn sounds before they read stories. The Qaida works the same way for the Quran. Arabic sounds first, Mushaf second. When parents skip this stage, I see the same story play out again and again. The child guesses. They stumble. Lessons become something to dread. Not because the child is weak, but because nobody built the foundation first.

Why Not Open the Quran Straight Away?

Parents ask me this in almost every trial lesson, so here is my straight answer.

Pronunciation first, everything else second

Arabic has sounds that English does not. The throat letter ع, Ayn. The heavy letter ص, Saad. Teach them wrong, and a child will repeat the mistake a thousand times before anyone catches it. The Qaida teaches the makhraj, the place each sound comes from, right at the start, while habits are still soft and easy to shape. Trust me, it is far easier to learn a sound correctly than to unlearn it later.

Confidence is everything

Watch a six year old finish the Qaida and pick up the Quran to read real words by themselves. Their whole face lights up. That feeling is worth more than any worksheet. A child who feels successful wants to come back. A child who feels lost finds excuses not to.

Tajweed needs a base to stand on

Tajweed is beautiful, but it is rules about sounds. Give those rules to a child who already reads fluently, and they click into place. Give them to a child still wrestling with the alphabet, and they sink. I tell parents the Qaida is the soil and Tajweed is the tree. No soil, no tree. Simple as that.

Small wins keep children going

Short lessons. Visible progress. A child who sees themselves improving week after week starts to enjoy the process, and that enjoyment is what carries them through Nazra, through Tajweed, and for some children, all the way through Hifz. It all starts with feeling that learning is possible.

Allah says in the Quran:

وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ

"And We have certainly made the Quran easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?" (Quran 54:17)

For a child, the Qaida is where that promised ease first becomes real.

What Happens Inside the Book

The Qaida builds in a fixed order. Each part only works because the part before it did its job.

1. The Arabic Alphabet (Huroof-e-Tahajji)

Twenty nine letters. Names and sounds, drilled until they are instant. I am strict about this in my lessons, in a kind way. I do not want a child who can sing the alphabet. I want a child who can look at any letter, in any order, and say it without a pause. That instant recognition is the backbone of everything that follows.

2. Points of Articulation (Makharij)

Where does each sound come from? Throat, tongue, lips, nose? This is where reading turns from approximate to correct. Children learn here that س, soft "seen", and ص, heavy "saad", are genuinely different letters, not close cousins. I use mouth-shape pictures for this, because a child grasps where the tongue goes from one picture far faster than from a long explanation.

3. Vowel Marks (Harakat)

Fatha, damma, kasra. Three little marks that change everything. Ba, bi, bu, practised until the combinations roll off the tongue without thought. Is it repetition? Of course. But when a teacher notices every small improvement and says so, children enjoy it. They like being good at something.

4. Sukoon, Shaddah, and Joining Letters

Things get fun here. Sukoon, a letter with no vowel. Shaddah, a letter doubled with force. Then joining letters into words, because Arabic letters change shape with their position. Two letters, then three, then longer words. This is the stage where children start to feel like real readers, and you can see it in how they sit up straighter.

5. Tanween, Madd, and Basic Rules

The final stretch: tanween, the double vowel, madd, the stretched sound, and the first gentle rules for the letter noon. A small taste of Tajweed, in other words. And the book closes with short verses from the Quran itself. So a child does not just finish a primer. They finish it reading the words of Allah. That matters.

Timeframe? Two to three classes a week, and most children are done in 3 to 6 months. Quicker for some, slower for others. Neither is a problem. Your child is not in a race with anyone.

When to Start

Around 4 to 5 is the usual advice, and it is good advice. At that age children can focus for a short lesson, follow instructions, and absorb new sounds almost effortlessly. Their ears are sharp, and that early clarity in pronunciation stays with them.

But late is fine too. I have started older children and adults with the same book, and they have done beautifully. The real question is not age at all. It is readiness. Can your child sit with a patient teacher for 20 to 30 minutes? If the answer is yes, then now is the right time.

Inside an Online Lesson

So what actually happens when your child logs on? Let me walk you through it, because parents in the UK, USA, Canada, Australia and Europe often picture something far more formal than the reality.

Your child meets me on Zoom or Google Meet, one on one, for 25 to 30 minutes. Just us. I share a colourful digital Qaida on the screen and highlight the letters as we go, so your child always knows where to look. I say a sound. They copy it. We practise, kindly, until it is solid. I hear every sound your child makes, because there is no one else in the lesson, so I can correct a slip immediately, before it settles into a habit. Then a short homework, 5 to 10 minutes of revision with a parent, before next time.

Parents are welcome to sit in, especially with younger children. And you get progress reports, so you are never left wondering where your child stands or what comes next.

What You Need

A phone, tablet or laptop with a camera. Internet that works. A quiet corner. Done. No books to buy, no school run, no rearranging your evening.

A Few Things That Help at Home

Lessons teach. Home makes it stick. Ten minutes of revision a day will do more than an hour once a week, I promise you. Sit nearby if you can. Listen. Children read with more care when someone they love is listening.

Celebrate the small stuff. Alphabet done? Make a fuss. Harakat section finished? Tell the family. Children chase praise, and praise for Quran progress is the best kind there is.

Please do not compare. Not with a sibling. Not with a cousin. Not with the neighbour's child who finished in three months. Comparison turns something sacred into a competition, and that resentment is very hard to undo.

And when your child struggles, because they will, some days, remind them of this. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the one who recites the Quran with difficulty, stammering through it, earns a double reward (Sahih al-Bukhari 4937, Sahih Muslim 798). Tell them that on a hard day. Watch what it does to their confidence.

Frequently Asked Questions

At what age should my child start learning the Noorani Qaida?

Four to five years old is ideal, when a child can focus for 20 to 30 minutes and follow simple instructions. Older children and adults start with the Qaida as well, so it is genuinely never too late, and I adjust the pace to each student.

Who will teach my child?

I will, personally. I am M Muddasir Hameed, the founder of Noor E Quran Institute, and I am the institute's only teacher. Lessons are private and one-on-one, so sisters and young girls learn in a comfortable setting that respects Islamic etiquette, with a parent welcome to sit in.

How does the free 3-day trial work, and what does it cost afterwards?

Your child receives three full one-on-one trial classes, completely free, with no payment and no obligation, so you can see the teaching style before deciding. After the trial, the monthly fee depends on how many classes per week you choose, and current plans are on the packages page.

How many classes per week does my child need?

Two to three 30-minute classes a week works for most children. It keeps the learning fresh without pressure, and a few minutes of revision at home each day multiplies the benefit of every class.

Conclusion

Small book. A few months. A lifetime of reading the Quran well. That is what is at stake in the beginning, which is why the beginning deserves a teacher who treats it seriously. If you would like your child to start that way, book a free 3-day trial class at Noor E Quran Institute. We begin with the very first letter, and we go from there, together.

title: Wudu and Salah: A Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners
metaDescription: Learn wudu and salah step by step: how to make wudu correctly, what breaks it, the 5 daily prayers with fard rakats, and how to pray 2 rakats properly.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Here is the honest truth about prayer: it starts before you even stand up. You wash, then you pray. Wudu, then salah. Five times a day, same rhythm, and honestly? Once somebody shows you properly, the whole thing clicks a lot faster than you expect.

Who is this for? Pretty much everyone I teach. The new Muslim staring at a prayer mat wondering where to begin. The mum or dad who wants their child to learn it right the first time. The brother or sister coming back after a long time away and feeling rusty. Whatever your starting point, this guide covers it: wudu done right, what actually breaks it, all five prayers and their fard rakats, two rakats walked through slowly, the slip-ups I keep seeing in beginners, and teaching kids without turning it into a battle. One note before we start: this is mainstream Sunni practice. Little details do vary between schools, I will point those out as we go, but the foundation never changes.

What Is Wudu?

Wudu is how you get ready to stand before Allah. Certain parts of the body, washed in a certain order, with clean water, and with the intention that this is for worship. Skip it and the prayer does not count. That single rule should tell you everything about how important it is.

There is a second side to it, though, one people only notice once they practise it. Wudu forces you to slow down. Phone down, sleeves up, water running, and suddenly you are actually present: your hands, your face, your feet, one thing at a time. "Cleanliness is half of faith," the Prophet ﷺ said (Sahih Muslim 223). Whenever I teach wudu, that hadith comes back to me, because it captures exactly why this washing feels nothing like an ordinary wash.

The Quran gives us the core of wudu in one verse:

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصَّلَاةِ فَاغْسِلُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ وَأَيْدِيَكُمْ إِلَى الْمَرَافِقِ وَامْسَحُوا بِرُءُوسِكُمْ وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ إِلَى الْكَعْبَيْنِ

"O you who have believed, when you rise to perform prayer, wash your faces and your forearms to the elbows and wipe over your heads and wash your feet to the ankles." (Quran 5:6)

Everything obligatory is in that verse. Around it, the Sunnah adds the recommended touches: begin with Bismillah, wash each part three times, keep the order.

How to Make Wudu: Step by Step

Intention first, in your heart. No special words needed, no announcement. Just be clear to yourself: I am making wudu now. Then take the steps in order, one after another:

  1. Bismillah. Say "In the name of Allah" and begin.
  2. Hands, three times. Wash both hands up to the wrists, and let the water run between your fingers.
  3. Mouth, three times. Take water in, swirl it, spit it out.
  4. Nose, three times. Sniff a little water in gently, then blow it out. No need to force it.
  5. Face, three times. Hairline to chin, ear to ear. Be honest with yourself about the edges.
  6. Arms, three times each. Right first, all the way up to and including the elbows. Check for dry patches.
  7. Head, once. Wipe over it with wet hands, front to back. This is called Masah.
  8. Ears. Index fingers inside, thumbs behind, one wipe.
  9. Feet, three times each. Right first, up to and including the ankles, and get between the toes.

Done? Then say the testimony of faith, as recommended: "Ash-hadu an la ilaha ill-Allah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh."

Where do beginners usually slip up? Two places, in my experience. First, water: people run the tap full blast, when the Prophet ﷺ managed with barely a handful. A gentle, steady flow does the job. Second, dry skin they never noticed. Waterproof nail polish is a barrier, so off it comes. And then the usual suspects, the spots everyone misses: between the toes, the heels, the elbows. Slow down for those three and you are covered.

What Breaks Wudu?

Good news: wudu lasts. It stays with you until one of these happens:

  • Passing wind, urinating, or defecating
  • Deep sleep (dozing lightly while sitting upright does not break it, in the view of many scholars)
  • Losing consciousness
  • A heavy flow of blood, pus, or vomit

That is it. If one of those happens, renew your wudu before praying. You only need a full bath, ghusl, for major impurity, which is a different matter altogether.

What Is Salah?

Now salah, the prayer itself, five times a day, the second pillar of Islam. Standing, reciting, bowing, prostrating. No middleman, just you speaking to Allah directly. I know five times a day sounds heavy when you are new. Live it for a few weeks, though, and it flips: those five pauses become the skeleton your whole day hangs on, not an interruption to it.

The five prayers, with their obligatory (fard) rakats:

Prayer Time Fard Rakats
Fajr Dawn, before sunrise 2
Dhuhr Midday, after the sun passes its zenith 4
Asr Afternoon, before sunset 4
Maghrib Just after sunset 3
Isha Night, after twilight disappears 4

One rakat is a single unit: stand, recite, bow, prostrate, sit. Sunnah prayers sit around the fard ones, and you can build up to them once the obligatory prayers feel solid.

Allah commands us to guard the prayers:

حَافِظُوا عَلَى الصَّلَوَاتِ وَالصَّلَاةِ الْوُسْطَىٰ وَقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قَانِتِينَ

"Maintain with care the obligatory prayers and in particular the middle prayer, and stand before Allah, devoutly obedient." (Quran 2:238)

Just starting out? Then forget everything optional for now. Fard only. Get those steady, get them comfortable, and trust me, the recitation sorts itself out over weeks of practice. Worrying about it does not.

How to Pray Salah: Step by Step (Two Rakats)

Before the first Allahu Akbar, run through this little checklist. Wudu, done. Body and clothes, clean. Facing the Qibla, toward the Kaaba in Makkah. Prayer time, actually started, not guessed. And dress: women cover everything except face and hands, men cover navel to knees at minimum, shoulders covered too.

Now Fajr, two rakats, from start to finish:

  1. Niyyah. Intend in your heart which prayer this is.
  2. Takbir. Hands up to ear level, "Allahu Akbar." Allah is Greatest, and everything else waits now.
  3. Fold your hands. Right over left, on the chest, or below the navel in some schools.
  4. Opening dua (recommended). "Subhanak-Allahumma wa bihamdika, wa tabarak-asmuka, wa ta'ala jadduka, wa la ilaha ghayruk." Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise.
  5. Al-Fatihah. Start with isti'adhah and Bismillah, then the whole surah. You will recite this in every single rakat, so it is worth learning well.
  6. Another surah. Any short one you know, Al-Ikhlas for example. Note: in the third and fourth rakats of longer prayers, you recite only Al-Fatihah.
  7. Ruku. "Allahu Akbar," bow, hands on knees, back flat, and say "Subhana Rabbiyal-'Adhim" three times.
  8. Stand up. "Sami' Allahu liman hamidah," then, standing straight, "Rabbana wa lakal-hamd."
  9. Sujud. "Allahu Akbar," down to the ground: forehead, nose, both hands, knees, toes. Say "Subhana Rabbiyal-A'la" three times.
  10. Sit, then prostrate again. A short sit, then a second sujud with the same words.
  11. Second rakat. Stand up and repeat steps 5 to 10.
  12. Final sitting. Tashahhud, ending with the testimony: none worthy of worship but Allah, and Muhammad His servant and Messenger.
  13. Salawat. Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, the Durood-e-Ibrahim.
  14. Taslim. Turn right: "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah." Turn left, same words. Prayer complete.

Longer prayers? Same pattern, one extra bit: sit for Tashahhud after the second rakat, stand for the remaining rakats, then the final sitting before Taslim. That is all. And if you are still wondering which prayer to learn first, take Fajr. Two rakats, the simplest shape there is, and the easiest to hold in your memory.

Common Beginner Mistakes

  • Speed. Rushing through positions is the number one problem. The Prophet ﷺ corrected a man for praying too fast. Stillness in each position is part of the prayer, not a delay to it.
  • Weak Al-Fatihah. Since it appears in every rakat, this surah deserves your first effort. Get it right, then move on.
  • Sloppy wudu. Dry heels, dry toes. A thirty-second check at the end fixes most of it.
  • Wrong time. Every prayer has a window. Learn the rough times for your city and you avoid this entirely.
  • All or nothing thinking. Missing a prayer hurts more than reciting imperfectly. Pray, even while you are still learning.
  • Trying to master everything in week one. Fard first. Sunnah later. Longer surahs later still.

Tips for Teaching Kids

  • Keep it happy. Start young, let toddlers copy you, and let prayer feel like a good part of the day, not a lecture.
  • Show, do not just tell. Do wudu in front of them, slowly, naming each step out loud.
  • Put up charts. A simple step chart by the bathroom and another by the prayer mat does more than repeated reminders.
  • One surah at a time. Al-Fatihah first, then short surahs. Short daily repetition beats a long weekly session.
  • Notice the effort. A prayer on time, a new dua learned: celebrate it. That is how habits form.
  • Pray as a family. One prayer a day together, and children absorb the habit without being pushed.
  • Get one good teacher. At Noor E Quran Institute, I teach every lesson myself, M Muddasir Hameed, the founder, in private 1-on-1 classes. One teacher from start to finish means pronunciation and order are corrected properly, lesson after lesson.

So that is the rhythm, start to finish. Wash, then pray, five times a day. On paper it looks long. In real life, practised daily, it turns into second nature quicker than most people believe. And remember: every person who prays confidently today once stood exactly where you are standing now.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who will teach me or my child?

M Muddasir Hameed, the founder of Noor E Quran Institute, teaches every lesson himself in private 1-on-1 classes. No teacher rotation, no handovers: the same teacher follows you or your child from the first lesson onward. And you can begin with a free 3-day trial class, with no commitment.

How much do online Quran classes cost?

The fee is monthly, and it depends on how many classes per week you choose. We confirm the exact fee with you before enrolment, so nothing comes as a surprise, and the free 3-day trial comes first either way.

Can sisters learn comfortably and privately?

Yes. Every lesson is a private 1-on-1 session from home, so there is no group class and no one else present. Sisters learn in full privacy, family members can sit nearby if they wish, and the founder teaches every student with the same care and respect.

Do I need wudu before every prayer?

Only a new wudu when the old one breaks. One wudu can carry you through several prayers. When it breaks, renew it, it takes a couple of minutes, and pray.

title: What Is Tajweed and Why Does It Matter in Quran Recitation?
metaDescription: Wondering what is Tajweed? Learn the meaning of Tajweed, its history, the Prophet's recitation, and why correct Quran recitation matters for every Muslim.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
So what is Tajweed, really?

Not singing. Not a scholars-only subject. Just this: reading the Quran the way it was revealed. Each letter from its right place, held for the right time, stopped in the right spot.

That is the whole thing. And it matters more than most parents realise, because a child reading the Quran is either reading it right or slightly wrong, and in Arabic, slightly wrong can mean a different word entirely. A throat sound swapped for another. A short vowel stretched too long. Suddenly the meaning has shifted. Sometimes to the opposite of what was intended. With Allah's words, that is not a small matter.

The Word Gives It Away

Tajweed comes from jawwada. Doing something well. Beautifying it. Bringing it to its best.

Before it is a set of rules, then, it is an attitude. Be careful with this. Do not rush it. Honestly, a child who grasps only that will already be ahead of many adults.

Scholars define it tighter, of course. Every letter gets its full rights and dues. Its proper place in the mouth or throat. Its proper qualities. Its proper length, not a beat more or less. Its proper pause. Put that together and the reading comes out clear, steady, quietly beautiful. Not flashy. Steady is the word I keep coming back to.

One confusion I hear constantly: people think Tajweed means a beautiful voice. It does not. A nice voice is a gift, full stop, and a lovely thing to hear. But I would take a plain voice that reads every letter correctly over a gorgeous voice that mangles them, every single time. The first person is reciting better. That is not a controversial opinion among teachers. It is just how it works.

How It All Began: Listening

Here is something people forget. Tajweed did not start as a book. It started as listening.

Jibril recited to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ recited it straight back, exactly as he heard it. The Companions learned from him in person, sound by sound, pause by pause. No textbook. No diagram. Just ears, and care.

Then Islam spread, and spread fast. New Muslims from Persia, Africa, Central Asia, people whose own languages had no throat letters at all, were reading the Quran and, understandably, getting some sounds wrong. Not carelessly. They simply had never made those sounds before.

So early scholars wrote down what teachers had always taught by ear. Where letters come from. Which sounds blend. How long to hold a sound. Where to stop. Later, scholars of the qira'at, the canonical readings, Imam Ibn al-Jazari is the name most students meet first, organised everything into a system, so a learner hundreds of years later could still read the way the Prophet ﷺ read.

Stop and think about that chain. Teacher, student, teacher, student, unbroken, back to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Your child, learning Tajweed now, steps into that chain. I find that genuinely moving, and I have been teaching a long time.

How the Prophet ﷺ Read It

The descriptions from his Companions are strikingly simple. Slow. Measured. Moving.

He ﷺ read slowly enough that each letter could be heard on its own. He paused at verse endings. He stretched a sound when it needed stretching, and stopped exactly there. Umm Salamah described his reading as clear, letter by letter. He ﷺ also told his followers to beautify their recitation, because making the Quran sound pleasant honours it.

Allah commands this style directly, in words every Tajweed teacher quotes:

وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا

"And recite the Quran with measured, deliberate recitation." (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4)

One verse, and really the whole subject is in it. Unhurried. Precise. Thoughtful. The Quran describes itself the same way, as "a blessed Book which We have revealed to you, so that they may reflect upon its verses" (Surah Sad, 38:29). Reflection needs time. You cannot reflect on a verse you have just sprinted through.

Why Bother? Three Honest Reasons

Parents ask me this outright, and good for them. Why does the detail matter?

1. A Tiny Slip Changes the Word

Take those throat letters again. English does not have them, so a new reader can easily swap one for another and never notice. Or stretch a short vowel, and the word becomes something else. Something sometimes unsuitable. Nobody means to do it. Tajweed stops it happening by accident. That is why scholars call learning enough Tajweed to avoid meaning-changing mistakes an obligation for every reciter, not an optional interest.

2. The Quran Deserves Better Than a Rush

It is the speech of Allah. Think how carefully you would speak to a person you respect deeply. You would not mumble their name or rush past what you meant to say. Allah's words deserve at least that care, and more. Slowing down, shaping each letter, following the rules of reading, that is reverence, not pedantry. And children copy what they see far quicker than what they are told, so the example matters.

3. Salah Changes

We read mostly in prayer, five times a day, day after day. When the reading is right and unhurried, prayer feels different. Less like a race through familiar verses. More like actually being there, word by word, letter by letter. Parents tell me this is usually the first change they spot in their children. Quieter prayer. Slower prayer. Prayer that feels real.

And Then There Are the Side Effects

Correctness is only the start. Families are often surprised by what comes next.

Reward, for one. The Prophet ﷺ taught that a skillful reciter will be with the noble, righteous angels, while the person who reads with difficulty, stumbling and trying again, receives double reward. The struggle counts. It is not wasted. He ﷺ also said, "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it" (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027). Note both halves of that. The learner and the teacher. The child and the parent who made the lesson happen.

Memorisation, for another. Verses learned right stick. Verses learned wrong have to be unlearned, and unlearning is miserable, slow work. Every Hifz student knows this, usually from experience.

Then confidence. A child who knows their reading is correct will read aloud, lead a prayer, help a younger sibling, without that anxious knot. And once Tajweed is habit, it stays. Ramadan, prayer, a difficult night, every verse for the rest of their life will be read correctly. The slower pace also leaves room for tadabbur, deep reflection, because the meanings finally get a chance to sink in.

It Is Easier Than the Words Make It Sound

Makharij. Sifaat. Ghunnah. Yes, the vocabulary sounds intimidating. Like a university course you never signed up for.

The reality is much simpler, and much more like childhood itself. Listen. Copy. Get corrected, gently. Try again. One day the right sound is simply how you read, and you cannot remember when it clicked. No exam first. No list to memorise before opening the Quran.

Which brings me to why one to one teaching fits Tajweed so well. A teacher hears every letter and corrects you immediately. A book cannot hear you. An app cannot hear you, whatever its adverts claim. If you want to learn tajweed online, look for live listening, sound by sound, from a real teacher. At Noor E Quran Institute, that teacher is me, M Muddasir Hameed, the founder, teaching every student myself, one at a time, no substitutes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Tajweed obligatory for every Muslim?

Here is the distinction scholars draw, and it is a helpful one. Learning enough to avoid mistakes that change the meaning is considered obligatory. Mastering every fine detail is recommended and richly rewarded, but it takes longer. So start where you are, find a teacher, and improve lesson by lesson. That is the whole path, really.

Do I need a beautiful voice to learn Tajweed?

No. I will say it again, because people do not believe it at first. No. Tajweed is about correct sounds, not impressive ones. Plenty of deeply respected reciters have ordinary voices. Their excellence is precision, not prettiness. Your voice, as it is, can carry a correct, dignified recitation.

How much do Tajweed classes cost, and is there a free trial?

Fees depend on how many classes you take each week, so the exact monthly fee is confirmed when you choose a schedule on the packages page. Every new student starts with a free 3-day trial, so you can try the classes before paying anything.

Who teaches the classes, and is learning from home comfortable for sisters?

All classes are taught by the founder, M Muddasir Hameed, himself, in private one to one lessons from your own home. Sisters learn in privacy, with family welcome to sit nearby, and parents can observe their children's lessons.

Take the First Step

Tajweed, then, is not some advanced extra for a few keen people. It is how the Quran was meant to be read, by everyone who reads it. The word means making something beautiful and perfect. The Prophet ﷺ read slowly and precisely. The rules guard Allah's words from accidental change, one sound at a time.

Every letter you fix brings you closer to reading as he ﷺ read. Start small if you need to. Just start.

title: 6 Kalimas Every Muslim Should Memorize
metaDescription: Memorize the 6 kalimas with easy transliteration and simple English meanings. Discover their virtues, practical learning tips, and how to teach them to kids.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Yes, every Muslim should know the six kalimas by heart, along with what they mean. They are six short Arabic phrases that sum up the core beliefs of Islam, and this guide gives you all six with clear transliteration and a plain English meaning, so you can learn them properly and teach them to your children with understanding.

Talk to Muslim parents about what they want most for their children, and one wish comes up again and again: that the words of faith sit naturally on their child's tongue and settle deep in their heart. Down the generations, families have passed the kalimas to little ones among the very first religious words they ever hear, side by side with the duas said each morning and night. Still, a good number of grown-ups never got the chance to learn them properly, new Muslims in particular, and anyone whose upbringing included little formal Islamic teaching. If that describes you, there is nothing to be embarrassed about, and starting now is perfectly fine.

What Are the Six Kalimas?

"Kalima" (plural: kalimat) is just the Arabic word for a "word" or "phrase". The six kalimas are six brief statements taken from the Quran and from what the Prophet ﷺ taught. Every one of them states something central to Islam: Allah alone is worthy of worship, Muhammad ﷺ is His Messenger, all praise belongs to Allah, and a believer keeps returning to Allah asking forgiveness.

Taken together, they pack the whole faith into a handful of lines. Belief, praise, oneness, forgiveness, protection from disbelief, all short enough to slip into your daily dhikr without any effort. Small children beginning their Islamic studies benefit from them, and so do adults patching holes in what they were taught years ago. Here they are, one at a time.

Before the list itself, one verse sums up the heart of all six better than pages of explanation could. Allah says in the Quran:

Arabic: قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ، اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ، لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ، وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ

Translation: "Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent." (Surah Al-Ikhlas, 112:1-4)

Hold that verse in your head as you work down the list. Each kalima below comes back to the same point in its own way: Allah is One, and worship belongs to Him alone.

The First Kalima: Tayyibah (The Pure Word)

Arabic: لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ مُحَمَّدٌ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ

Transliteration: Lā ilāha illallāhu Muḥammadur Rasūlullāh

Meaning: Nothing deserves to be worshipped except Allah, and Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah.

Everything else rests on this: Allah is One, and Muhammad ﷺ is His Messenger. A Muslim child hears it before almost anything else, and a believer hopes, by Allah's mercy, that it will be the last thing he ever says. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever's last words are 'La ilaha illallah' will enter Paradise." (Sunan Abi Dawud, 3116) If you need one reason to put this kalima first on your child's tongue and keep it firm in your own heart, that hadith is reason enough.

The Second Kalima: Shahadah (The Testimony)

Arabic: أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ

Transliteration: Ash-hadu allā ilāha illallāh, wa ash-hadu anna Muḥammadar Rasūlullāh

Meaning: I bear witness that nothing deserves worship except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah.

Where the first kalima states the belief, this one owns it. A person says these words on entering Islam, and then says them again in the tashahhud of every prayer for the rest of his life. "I bear witness" takes something you believe quietly inside and turns it into a stand you take in the open.

The Third Kalima: Tamjeed (The Glorification)

Arabic: سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَلَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَاللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ وَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ

Transliteration: Subḥānallāhi wal-ḥamdu lillāhi wa lā ilāha illallāhu wallāhu akbar, wa lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāhil-ʿaliyyil-ʿaẓīm

Meaning: Allah is free of every flaw and shortcoming, all praise belongs to Him alone, nothing deserves worship except Him, and He is greater than everything. No one has any strength or ability except through Allah, the Most High, the Almighty.

You will recognise the best loved phrases of dhikr sitting together here: "SubhanAllah", "Alhamdulillah", "Allahu Akbar". Then the kalima adds the part that slips our minds most, that every ounce of strength comes from Allah alone. Allah says: "Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest." (Quran, 13:28) Saying this kalima is that rest, in a single breath.

The Fourth Kalima: Tawheed (The Oneness)

Arabic: لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ يُحْيِي وَيُمِيتُ وَهُوَ حَيٌّ لَا يَمُوتُ أَبَدًا أَبَدًا ذُو الْجَلَالِ وَالْإِكْرَامِ بِيَدِهِ الْخَيْرُ وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ

Transliteration: Lā ilāha illallāhu waḥdahū lā sharīka lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-ḥamd, yuḥyī wa yumīt, wa huwa ḥayyul-lā yamūt, abadan abada, dhul-jalāli wal-ikrām, bi-yadihil-khayr, wa huwa ʿalā kulli shay'in qadīr

Meaning: Nothing deserves worship except Allah alone. He has no partner or rival. Everything in existence belongs to Him, and all praise is His. He gives life and He takes it away. He is the Living One who never dies. He is full of majesty and honour, all goodness is in His hand, and He has power over everything.

No other kalima is this long or this detailed. On its own it reads like a short creed: who owns everything, who gives life and takes it, and whose hand holds all good. Take it in pieces rather than all at once, clause by clause, and let what each part means pull the words along behind it. Grasp the clauses and the Arabic comes much more readily.

The Fifth Kalima: Istighfar (Seeking Forgiveness)

Arabic: أَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ رَبِّي مِنْ كُلِّ ذَنْبٍ أَذْنَبْتُهُ عَمْدًا أَوْ خَطَأً سِرًّا أَوْ عَلَانِيَةً وَأَتُوبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنَ الذَّنْبِ الَّذِي أَعْلَمُ وَمِنَ الذَّنْبِ الَّذِي لَا أَعْلَمُ إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ وَسَتَّارُ الْعُيُوبِ وَغَفَّارُ الذُّنُوبِ وَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ

Transliteration: Astaghfirullāha rabbī min kulli dhanbin adhnabtuhū ʿamdan aw khaṭa'an sirran aw ʿalāniyyah, wa atūbu ilayh, minadh-dhanbil-ladhī aʿlam, wa minadh-dhanbil-ladhī lā aʿlam, innaka anta ʿallāmul-ghuyūb, wa sattārul-ʿuyūb, wa ghaffārudh-dhunūb, wa lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāhil-ʿaliyyil-ʿaẓīm

Meaning: I ask Allah, my Lord, to forgive me for every sin I have committed, whether on purpose or by mistake, in private or in public. I turn back to Him, seeking forgiveness for the sins I remember and the sins I have forgotten. You alone know everything hidden, You cover up people's faults, and You forgive sins again and again. No one has strength except through Allah, the Most High, the Almighty.

Look at how wide this kalima casts its net. Deliberate sins and slips, sins done in private and in public, sins you remember and sins that have slipped your mind entirely, nothing is left out, and that is deliberate. Repentance is not only for the wrongs you can list; it covers the ones you have forgotten as well. Making this a nightly habit, just before sleep, is one of the best routines a family can build.

The Sixth Kalima: Radd-e-Kufr (Rejecting Disbelief)

Arabic: اَللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ أَنْ أُشْرِكَ بِكَ شَيْئًا وَأَنَا أَعْلَمُ وَأَسْتَغْفِرُكَ لِمَا لَا أَعْلَمُ تُبْتُ عَنْهُ وَتَبَرَّأْتُ مِنْ كُلِّ دِينٍ سِوَى دِينِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَأَسْلَمْتُ وَقُلْتُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ مُحَمَّدٌ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ

Transliteration: Allāhumma innī aʿūdhu bika min an ushrika bika shay'an wa anā aʿlam, wa astaghfiruka limā lā aʿlam, tubtu ʿanhu wa tabarra'tu min kulli dīnin siwā dīnil-islām, wa aslamtu wa qultu: lā ilāha illallāh Muḥammadur Rasūlullāh

Meaning: O Allah, I seek protection with You from associating anything with You while I know it, and I ask Your forgiveness for whatever I do not realize. I have turned away from it completely and I distance myself from every religion other than Islam. I have submitted myself to You, and I say: nothing deserves worship except Allah, and Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah.

Think of this final kalima as a guard against shirk, the gravest sin in Islam, and notice how it ends: with belief declared all over again. Said morning and evening, it renews the commitment daily. It is a fitting place to finish. The set opens with belief, and it closes with belief protected.

How to Memorize the Six Kalimas

Taking on all six in one go is too much for most children, and honestly for most adults as well. A slower path works far better:

  • Begin with the shortest. Get the first kalima down in one day. Its words are probably already familiar to you from prayer.
  • Take on one new kalima each week. Say the new one ten times after every prayer, and keep going over the earlier ones as you go.
  • Understand it before you memorise it. Once the meaning is clear, the Arabic stays in your memory much longer than sounds learned without understanding.
  • Copy a correct recitation. Listen to a trustworthy reciter or your teacher, and check how you sound, above all on the longer kalimas.
  • Learn with someone else. When a parent and child revise together, revision stops feeling like homework and becomes time spent together.
  • Go over them every week. Even when all six are memorised, run through them together each Friday so they never slip away.

For anyone only just beginning to read Arabic, a grounding in Noorani Qaida first changes everything, because the letters and vowel marks will already look familiar instead of the kalimas being a string of sounds to copy blindly.

Think of the six kalimas as companions for life: some of the earliest words many of us ever learn, and words we hope to repeat right up to our last breath. Learn them with their meanings, pass them to your children gently, and let them settle into your daily dhikr.

Frequently Asked Questions

At what age should children learn the kalimas?

Four or five is a good age to begin with the first kalima, next to the short duas said every day. There is no fixed rule, though. As soon as your child can copy short phrases back to you, you can start, one kalima at a time, in short and happy sessions. Notice the effort, not just the accuracy.

Do I need to learn the Arabic, or is the translation enough?

The Arabic matters, because the kalimas are meant to be said in their own wording, and they turn up in daily dhikr. But the wording on its own is not enough: without the meaning, the words stay hollow. That is why this guide always gives you both together.

How long does it take to memorize all six?

At one kalima a week with a little revision every day, most children have all six within about two months, and adults usually get there sooner. Short and steady wins: ten minutes daily does more than a single long session once a week.

Can my child learn the kalimas with a teacher at Noor E Quran Institute?

Yes. Every class at Noor E Quran Institute is taught by the founder himself, M Muddasir Hameed, one student at a time, so your child learns each kalima with correct pronunciation and real understanding. Sisters study in that same private setup, with complete privacy and ease. What you pay each month depends on how many classes you book per week, and a free 3-day trial class lets you see how the lessons run before making any decision.

title: 5 Simple Tajweed Rules Every Parent Should Teach
metaDescription: Learn 5 simple tajweed rules for kids that parents can teach at home, easy examples, fun practice tips, and simple ways to build correct Quran recitation.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
It happens in almost every home. Your kid sits down, reads a full page of the Quran from start to finish without a single stumble, and you feel this wave of actual pride. Then one letter just lands wrong. Not horribly wrong. Just a bit off. And you are sitting there thinking, I can hear that's not right, but honestly? I haven't got the foggiest idea how to fix it.

Here is the relief: you don't need to fix everything at once. Most of the weird little mistakes kids make come right back to the exact same five rules. Learn those five, mess around with them for a few minutes a day, and you'll hear a real shift within weeks. I teach these to my own students first thing because they work.

What Is Tajweed in Plain Words?

Tajweed simply means giving every letter its proper sound, its proper length, and its proper pause. Nothing mystical about it. Allah says in the Quran: "And recite the Quran with measured recitation" (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4). Slow, clear, measured. A Tajweed teacher will unpack miles more depth later on, but these five rules are where everything actually begins.

Rule 1: Ghunnah, the Sound That Hums

Turn this into a quick game right away. Ask your kid to hum like a bee. Nnnn. Put a finger right on the side of their nose. Can they feel that vibration? That buzz is Ghunnah.

It pops up whenever a noon (ن) or a meem (م) has a shaddah, that little w-shaped mark (ّ). The sound has to park in the nose for about two beats before you move on. Look at the very first word of Surah Al-Kawthar: إِنَّا. If the noon stays flat, the word is dead on arrival. Give it that nasal hum and it just opens right up. Read إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ الْكَوْثَر together and drag that buzz out a second. Kids think it's hilarious, which is why they actually remember it next time.

Rule 2: Qalqalah, Letters That Bounce

Five letters flat out refuse to sit still: ق ط ب ج د. Teachers group them into the phrase "qutb jad" so brains can grasp them. When one of these guys carries a sukoon (the small ْ mark), it shouldn't just die out flat. It bounces. It's got a tiny echo, like a tennis ball dropped once on a hard floor.

Surah Al-Ikhlas is packed with them. أَحَدٌ, الصَّمَدُ, يُولَدْ. That final daal in أَحَدٌ needs to pop gently. If your kid just swallows it, the word loses its whole tail. Try keeping a soft foam ball nearby during practice. Every single time a bouncing letter shows up, give a tiny bounce on the table. Silly? Totally. Effective? You bet. After a week, they'll spot Qalqalah letters before you even blink.

Rule 3: Madd, the Stretch

This is the one I correct non-stop: kids rushing long vowels. Arabic has short sounds and long sounds. The long ones, called Madd, demand a full two counts. An ا after a fatha is a long "aa". A و after a damma is "oo". A ي after a kasra is "ee".

Say قَالَ (qaala) out loud, then say it rushed and clipped. Your kid will hear it immediately. One sounds like talking, the other sounds like someone trying to ditch homework. The fix is stupidly simple. Hold up two fingers and count "one, two" on every long vowel. Some parents use a rubber band on long sounds and let it go slack on short ones. Whatever works. Just don't skip this, because rushed vowels quietly butcher more recitation than any tough letter ever could.

Rule 4: Ikhfa, the Letter That Hides

Sometimes a noon doesn't want to be loud. When a noon with a sukoon (نْ) sits right before certain letters, the n softens, half-hiding, sliding into the next sound with a light nasal brush instead of a hard stop.

Take أَنْتُمْ. Say it with a heavy, clunky English "an-tum" and it sounds awful. Let that noon melt instead, and the whole word smooths out. Turn it into hide-and-seek at the table. Cover the نْ with your thumb and ask where the n ran off to. Read it twice, once like a clunky robot with a hard n, once soft and breathy, and let your kid judge which one sounds right. They'll pick the soft one every time. Their own ear catching it matters way more than memorizing terminology.

Rule 5: Waqf, Knowing Where to Stop

Every verse wraps up with a tiny round sign, ۝. That's the literal stop sign of the Quran. Stop there, catch your breath, then keep going. What do kids usually do? They stop wherever they run out of air, often slicing right through the middle of a phrase and cutting the meaning in half.

Read قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ and halt completely at the sign. Notice how اللَّهُ and أَحَدٌ belong together, so pausing right between them sounds as weird as cutting off a mid-word break in English. Play red light, green light with this. They read, you raise your hand at every ۝, and they have to pause for a real breath. Race through Surah Al-Fatiha counting stops. A week of that and they handle it naturally.

Three Things That Actually Work at Home

Keep practice sessions tiny. Five genuinely focused minutes crush thirty dragging, miserable minutes every single time. Stick to one rule a week. Seriously, slower always wins.

When they miss a letter, skip the lecture. Just say the word right yourself, flash a quick smile, and let them echo you. Kids mimic whatever feels safe. Warm corrections feel like help, but sharp ones just feel like pressure.

And hey, learn out loud right beside them. You don't need to be an expert. A parent trying, occasionally messing up, and laughing it off teaches a lesson no book ever can: this Book is worth an adult's effort too.

Pick one rule this week. Just one. Play its little game after dinner, and just listen. If you ever want a real teacher to listen in and pinpoint what your kid needs, that's what we're here for, and the first three days at Noor E Quran Institute are a completely free trial.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to know Tajweed myself to teach my child?

Not at all, and most parents don't. Just stay one tiny step ahead by skimming that week's rule before they do, and leave the technical heavy lifting to their teacher. Home reinforcement plus proper guidance is the combo that wins.

At what age should children start learning Tajweed rules?

As soon as they're reading independently, usually right after finishing Noorani Qaida, around five to seven years old. Keep it light and game-based at that age, no heavy textbook theory. Little ears pick up sounds fast, so early habits mean fewer things to unlearn later.

My child already reads the Quran fluently. Is it too late to fix pronunciation?

Not even close. It's super common and totally fixable. A teacher usually hears just a few specific hitches in a fluent reader, not a total restart. Gentle fixes over a few weeks iron it right out.

How do online Quran classes help with Tajweed?

A live set of ears catches every single mistake the second it happens, stopping bad habits before they bake in. Apps can't do that. In our online Quran classes for kids, real-time feedback is baked into every session, and you can test-drive the first three days free to see how your child takes to it.

title: Quran Routine for Kids: How to Build a Daily Habit at Home
metaDescription: Build a daily Quran routine for kids with habit-based scheduling, sample timetables by age, progress charts, rewards that work, and tips for busy days.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Let me tell you what I actually see, week after week, in real families. The child is not the problem. The parents are not the problem either. The problem is that nobody decided when Quran time happens. So it gets pushed, and pushed, until bedtime arrives and everyone is too tired to argue about it. If you fix that one decision, when, the rest gets much easier. That is what this article is really about: building a daily Quran routine for kids that fits an ordinary, busy household, not an ideal one.

I have taught children in the UK, the US, Canada, and Australia, all online, all one to one, and the pattern is the same everywhere. School, homework, meals, activities, screens. The Quran has to compete with all of that, and a vague plan like "we will read sometime today" loses every time. A fixed time wins, even if it is only ten minutes. Especially if it is only ten minutes, because ten minutes is a promise a tired child can keep.

The Verse I Come Back To

There is a verse I quote to parents more than any other when we talk about routine. Allah says:

وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا

"And recite the Quran with measured recitation." (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4)

Measured. I love that word for this topic. It does not mean long. It does not mean impressive. It means steady, careful, unhurried. A little, done properly, every day. The Prophet, peace be upon him, put the value of this work simply: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027) A routine is how an ordinary family turns that into something daily, instead of something they mean to do.

Forget Motivation. Use a Trigger Instead

Ask any parent and they will tell you: Monday's enthusiasm is gone by Thursday. Children are like that. Adults are like that, if we are honest. So building Quran time on motivation is building on sand.

Build it on a trigger instead. A trigger is a moment that already happens, and you simply hang Quran time onto it. Fajr ends, book opens. School bag drops, book opens before the tablet comes out. Pyjamas on, one surah before sleep. No decision to make, no debate, because the moment itself reminds everyone. Finish the session before anyone gets fed up, with a sticker, a tick on a chart, or just a genuine "well done, that was good reading". Kids remember how a session ended. End it well, and they will come back tomorrow without a fight.

Short beats long here, every time. Fifteen minutes daily will beat a two hour weekend marathon, and not just because children concentrate better in short bursts. Daily reading keeps yesterday's lesson alive in their head. Skip three days and they feel like beginners again, which is miserable for a child. Keep the thread unbroken, even thinly, and fluency grows quietly, almost without anyone noticing, until one day the child reads a page they could not read last month.

Anchoring It to Salah, or to Whatever Already Works

For most of our families, salah times are the obvious anchors. Fajr is quiet, and new memorisation, the sabaq, sits well there, before the day gets noisy. After school or Asr catches a child who is still awake and alert, and it draws a line between school and home. Maghrib or bedtime is softer, better for revision, the sabqi, or for listening to a recitation together while the house winds down.

But here is my honest advice: use the anchor your family will keep, not the one that sounds most pious. I have seen Fajr routines collapse in homes where mornings are pure chaos, and I have seen bedtime routines thrive in those same homes, because bedtime was calm. Nobody gets a prize for choosing Fajr. You get the prize, if you like, for still doing it in three months. Say the time out loud, put it where everyone can see it, and then protect it like you would protect a class booking, because that is what it is.

By Age, Because a 5 Year Old Is Not a 12 Year Old

Ages 4 to 6: Around 15 Minutes, All of It Gentle

Little children need short, sweet, and repeated. Morning, about ten minutes: yesterday's Qaida page, point, repeat, praise, and stop while it is still fun. Bedtime, about five minutes: a short surah they already know, Al-Fatihah, Al-Ikhlas, and one dua, so they end the day feeling successful. That is it. Fifteen minutes total. At this age, the habit itself is the lesson. Pages will come later.

Ages 7 to 10: Around 30 Minutes, in Two Pieces

Now you can do more, but still split it. Twenty minutes after Fajr or after school for the Nazra lesson, new part slowly, then yesterday's part again until it flows. Ten minutes at bedtime for the week's surahs and duas. Children this age love to see progress, so let them see it: a chart, a checklist, a page count that climbs. And watch the clock honestly. A session that runs long stops teaching and starts annoying, and an annoyed child learns nothing, however good the lesson was.

Ages 11 and Up: 30 to 45 Minutes, With Their Input

Teenagers and older children can manage a fuller shape. Morning, fifteen to twenty minutes of new work, Nazra or Hifz sabaq. Evening, fifteen to twenty minutes of revision, recent lessons (sabqi) one day, older portions (manzil) the next, taking turns across the week. Once a week, a longer look back together. And please, ask them to help plan it. I say this from experience: a teenager who helped choose the time will defend it. A teenager who was simply told the time will find a hundred reasons it does not work.

Classes and Home Practice, Doing Different Jobs

Sometimes parents worry they are doubling up. They are not. In my lessons I teach the new material, I catch the mistakes, and I decide what comes next and how much. Home practice is where that material becomes fluent, because the child meets it again the next day, and again. One without the other is half a system.

Practically, that means: on a class day, go easy at home, ten to fifteen minutes revising what we did, and that is enough. On a non-class day, follow the age pattern above properly, so the next class begins with confidence, not with re-teaching. At the weekend, five minutes with the progress chart together, just to close the week and start the next one well. And tell me, as your child's teacher, what your home schedule looks like. If I know the real practice time, I can set the lesson size to match it, smaller in exam weeks, a little bigger in holidays. It is a small conversation that avoids a lot of silent stress.

Charts, Stickers, and Celebrating the Streak

I am a fan of simple tracking, because children cannot feel progress they cannot see. A sticker for each day done, and a small pre-agreed treat for a full week, a favourite dinner, a park visit, story time, whatever your family enjoys. For Nazra, a checklist of pages and surahs is surprisingly motivating; children love watching it fill up. When a milestone lands, a juz finished, a set of surahs learned, thirty days in a row, make a fuss, even a small one. Families remember what they celebrate, and children learn what matters by what gets celebrated.

One rule, though: reward the effort of showing up, not perfection. A month of daily reading, wobbly in places, beats one perfect recitation and three weeks of nothing. Praise the streak first. Fluency is what a streak produces, given time.

Bad Days, Holidays, and the Dreaded Slump

Every routine hits trouble, and the families who last are the ones who planned for it. On a crazy day, do five minutes. One page, one surah, one dua. That is not failure, that is the system working, because five minutes keeps the chain intact, and an intact chain is easy to resume. Travelling? Take a small mushaf, or a Quran app on your phone. Some of the best reading I have heard from students happened in airports, of all places, because the time was there and the app was ready. Ill or in exams? Drop to five minutes, drop the guilt, and tell your child the routine bends but does not break. They will remember that sentence long after they forget the schedule.

Slumps need a different touch. When a child digs their heels in, lecturing usually makes it worse. Try shrinking the session, moving it to another time, or letting them read to a younger sibling, which most older children secretly enjoy. Novelty restarts things. Pressure stalls them. I have watched that play out more times than I can count.

Conclusion

If I had to boil all of this down to one line for a busy parent, it would be this: pick one time, keep it short, and do not miss it. Anchor it to something you already do, match it to your child's age, track it simply, and let five minutes save the hard days. Do that for a few months, and you will notice something quietly wonderful. Quran time will stop feeling like another task, and start feeling like part of the day, which is exactly where it belongs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who teaches my child, exactly?

I do, personally. I am M Muddasir Hameed, the founder of Noor E Quran Institute, and every lesson is a private 1-on-1 class taught by me, so your child has one teacher who knows their level and their routine.

What is the monthly fee?

It is based on how many classes per week you choose, and we confirm the exact figure at enrolment. You pay for your chosen weekly plan, with no extra charges hidden in it.

Is there a free trial?

Yes, there is a free 3-day trial. Your child can try the private lessons, meet me as their teacher, and test a routine slot that works for your family before you commit.

How do private lessons work for sisters and daughters?

Lessons take place at home, one to one, with no group and no other students in the session. Sisters and daughters learn privately and comfortably, at a time the family chooses.

title: Quran Pronunciation Fix: A Makharij Correction Guide
metaDescription: Master Quran pronunciation with this simple Makharij guide: the 17 articulation points of Arabic letters, self-diagnosis tips, and daily practice exercises.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Here is the honest test. Say ص. Now say س. If they sound the same, or if ط keeps slipping out as ت, reading more pages will not solve it. The problem is not fluency at all. It is Makharij, where each letter actually comes from in your mouth and throat. Learn those places, and your recitation starts to change, sometimes faster than you expect.

Allah tells us not to rush the Quran:

وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا

"And recite the Quran with measured recitation." (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4)

Measured. Not fast, not showy. Just each letter from its right place. That is where Tajweed really begins, and it is also good news, because Makharij is physical. You can feel it. You can practise it in ten minutes a day. It is more like learning a sport than memorising a theory.

What Are Makharij?

Makhraj, plural Makharij, means "point of exit". One letter, one exit point. Simple idea, tricky in practice, because letters that sound alike to most ears come from different spots entirely. س is light, off the tongue tip. ص is heavy and full, from the same area but with a completely different mouth shape. ه is a soft breath from deep in the throat. ح is firmer, from the middle. Same neighbourhood, different houses.

Why does it matter so much? Because a letter from the wrong place can change a word's meaning. The classical scholars knew this, which is why they put correct articulation at the very bottom of Tajweed, as the foundation. Everything else sits on top of it.

The 17 Articulation Points in 5 Regions

Altogether, scholars count 17 Makharij in 5 regions: the oral cavity (Al-Jawf, 1), the throat (Al-Halq, 3), the tongue (Al-Lisan, 10), the lips (Ash-Shafatan, 2), and the nasal cavity (Al-Khashoom, 1). We will go from deepest to outermost, so you can follow along with your own mouth as you read.

1. Al-Jawf, the Oral Cavity (1 Makhraj)

The Jawf is just the open space inside your mouth and throat. It produces the three Madd letters, ا, و, ي, when the matching vowel comes first. Try "baaa". Stretch it. Nothing blocks the sound, it just rings out, wide and free. Most people go wrong by squeezing these letters in the throat or shoving them up the nose. Let them be open. That is the whole trick.

2. Al-Halq, the Throat (3 Makharij)

Three depths, two letters each. Deepest: ء and ه, say "ah" from as far down as you can get it. Middle: ع and ح. Put your hand on your throat for 'ayn, you should feel it buzz about halfway down. This pair gives non-Arabs the most grief, and honestly, it deserves the practice time. Highest: غ and خ, those gargling sounds where the throat meets the mouth. Whisper "ah, 'a, gha" slowly. Feel it climb. If all six come out sounding like one muddy noise, you have found your first job: separate them.

3. Al-Lisan, the Tongue (10 Makharij)

The tongue carries the biggest load. From back to front: ق (back of tongue, soft palate), ك (a touch forward, hard palate), then ج, ش, ي from the middle. ض comes from the tongue's edge against the upper molars, and yes, it is famously the hardest letter in Arabic. Then the tip letters: ل, ن, ر on the gums behind the upper front teeth; ت, د, ط at the teeth's base; ص, ز, س near the lower teeth with air slipping between; ظ, ذ, ث poking slightly between the teeth. Run through "qa, ka, ja, la, na, ra, ta, sa, tha" at a crawl and notice the contact point moving forward. That movement is the lesson, really.

4. Ash-Shafatan, the Lips (2 Makharij)

  • Both lips: ب (baa), م (meem), و (waw, when it is not a Madd letter). Waw rounds the lips without fully closing them.
  • Lower lip on upper teeth: ف (faa). Touch the lower lip lightly to the upper front teeth and breathe the air out.

5. Al-Khashoom, the Nasal Cavity (1 Makhraj)

The nose handles ghunnah, that nasal hum on noon and meem in certain Tajweed cases. Quick test: pinch your nose and say "nnn". The sound dies or warps, because noon's ghunnah lives in the nose. Held right, it lasts about two counts, smooth and controlled. Held wrong, it honks. You will know the difference the moment you hear it.

Self-Diagnosis: Hearing Your Own Pronunciation Errors

Blunt truth: you cannot fix what you cannot hear. So try these five checks, and be honest with yourself about the results.

  1. Record yourself. Read a page out loud. Listen tomorrow, next to a trusted reciter. The mistakes you glide over while reading will jump out at you on playback, I promise.
  2. Minimal pairs. Drill س vs ص, ت vs ط, ه vs ح, ك vs ق. If a pair sounds identical, one of the two is sitting in the wrong place.
  3. Mirror check. Stand in front of a mirror for ث, ذ, ظ, ف. For ث especially, if you cannot see your tongue between your teeth, it is wrong.
  4. Nose test. Pinch your nose on ghunnah verses. Sound collapses? Good, your ghunnah is genuinely nasal.
  5. Slow motion. Halve your speed. Give each letter its full Makhraj. Speed is a great hiding place for errors, slowness drags them into the open.

Daily Exercises to Strengthen Your Makharij

Ten to fifteen minutes a day. That is all. Short and daily wins over long and occasional, every time.

Exercise 1: The Throat Ladder

Repeat أ, ه, ع, ح, غ, خ ten times a day, slowly, feeling the sound climb from the bottom of the throat to the top. It targets the single most common fault I hear in non-native reciters, all the throat letters melted into one vague sound.

Exercise 2: Heavy vs. Light Letters

Seven letters stay "heavy" always: خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ (خص ضغط قظ). Drill the pairs س / ص, ت / ط, د / ض. Light means a smiling, empty mouth. Heavy means the mouth full, tongue raised. Overdo it at first. Looking silly for a week is a fair price for getting it right.

Exercise 3: The Qalqalah Bounce

Qalqalah letters, ق ط ب ج د (قطب جد), give a little echo on a sukoon: أَقْ، أَطْ، أَبْ، أَجْ، أَدْ. Little is the key word. A small echo, not a whole extra vowel.

Exercise 4: Ghunnah Control

Hold أَنْ، أَمْ with fingers resting lightly on your nose, two slow counts, then carry it into words like مِن، ثُمَّ. You want a smooth hum that sits inside the recitation, not something that takes over.

Exercise 5: The Daad Challenge

ض again, because it deserves its own drill. Side of the tongue hard against the upper molars, then a heavy "d": أَضْ. Twenty times a day, slowly. It is hard for almost everyone, so do not feel bad about it, just keep at it.

When to Get a Teacher's Help

Here is the limit of self-study, and I say this as a teacher: your own ears have blind spots. A trained teacher hears the 'ayn that is slightly off, the heavy letter that is almost but not quite heavy, the ghunnah held a beat too long. You have lived with those errors for years, so your brain files them as normal.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027) There is a reason learning and teaching sit together in that hadith. Recitation is passed ear to ear, not just page to eye.

So get help if the same letters still sound wrong on your recordings after a month, if heavy and light still blur, or if Hifz is on the horizon. Memorising a mistake just means unlearning it later, and that is far harder. At Noor E Quran Institute, I teach every class myself, and Makharij correction is part of each lesson, aimed at the exact letters a student struggles with.

Frequently Asked Questions

I do, personally. I am M Muddasir Hameed, the founder, and the only teacher at the institute. Lessons are private and one-on-one, so your child always learns with the same teacher, and you always know who that teacher is.

It depends on how many classes your child takes each week. The current plans are on the packages page, sibling discounts are available, and I will always give you the exact fee for your schedule before you enrol.

How does the free 3-day trial work?
