Is it private and comfortable for my daughter or for sisters learning?

Yes. Lessons are private, one-on-one, and at home, so your daughter learns somewhere familiar and comfortable. A parent or guardian is welcome to sit in on every lesson, and any concern comes straight to me.

Your Recitation Can Be Transformed

Strip Tajweed back and you find Makharij underneath it all. Every rule rests on letters coming from their rightful places. The map of 17 points is already in your mouth. This guide just helps you read it.

Start today, throat ladder first, then the heavy and light pairs, and record yourself once a week so you can hear the change. And when you want a trained ear beside you, book your free 3-day trial class at Noor E Quran Institute.

title: 40 Essential Daily Duas Every Muslim Should Know
metaDescription: Learn 40 essential daily duas for waking, eating, leaving home, sleeping, travel and more, with simple transliteration and easy English meanings for families.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Here are 40 duas, plain and simple, for the moments that make up a normal day. Waking up. Eating. Walking out of the door. Going to sleep. I have put them in that order, with the transliteration and what each one means in plain English, so a family can learn them together without a textbook.

You probably say a few already. Most of us do, Bismillah here, Alhamdulillah there, without ever counting them. Gathering them is not about the number. It is about noticing how much of the day can carry a dua.

Why Dua Comes First

Allah says in the Quran:

وَقَالَ رَبُّكُمُ ادْعُونِي أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ

“And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you.” (Surah Ghafir, 40:60)

And the Prophet ﷺ put it even shorter: “Supplication is worship.” (Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 3372) Think about that for a second. Eating becomes worship. Leaving the house becomes worship. Not because the act changed, but because you remembered Allah in it.

So take this list slowly. One part of the day at a time. A week on the morning duas, then the evening ones, then the rest. Forty sounds like a lot until you realise you already know five or six.

Waking Up

1. Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur: All praise is for Allah, who woke us after sleep; to Him we return.

2. Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi 'afani fi jasadi, wa radda 'alayya ruhi, wa adhina li bi dhikrih: All praise is for Allah, who kept my body well, returned my soul, and let me remember Him.

Say the first one while you are still sitting up. That is the whole trick. Tie the dua to the moment, not to a timetable.

Wudu

3. Bismillah: In the name of Allah.

4. Ash-hadu alla ilaha illallah, wahdahu la sharika lah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh: I testify none deserves worship but Allah alone, with no partner, and Muhammad ﷺ is His servant and Messenger.

Morning

5. Allahumma bika asbahna, wa bika amsayna, wa bika nahya, wa bika namutu, wa ilaykan-nushur: O Allah, by You we enter morning and evening; by You we live and die, and to You we return.

6. Allahumma inni as'aluka 'ilman nafi'an, wa rizqan tayyiban, wa 'amalan mutaqabbalan: O Allah, I ask You for useful knowledge, pure provision, and accepted deeds.

7. Raditu billahi rabban, wa bil-islami dinan, wa bi Muhammadin nabiyyan: I am pleased with Allah as my Lord, Islam as my religion, and Muhammad ﷺ as my Prophet.

8. Subhanallahi wa bihamdih: Glory be to Allah, and praise Him.

Three minutes. That is all the morning set takes once you know them, and it changes how the day starts.

Evening

9. Allahumma bika amsayna, wa bika asbahna, wa bika nahya, wa bika namutu, wa ilaykal-masir: O Allah, by You we enter evening and morning; by You we live and die, and to You is our final return.

10. A'udhu bikalimatillahit-tammati min sharri ma khalaq: I seek protection in Allah's perfect words from the evil of what He created.

11. Bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru ma'a ismihi shay'un fil-ardi wa la fis-sama', wa huwas-sami'ul-'alim: In Allah's name, with which nothing on earth or heaven can harm; He hears all and knows all.

12. Amsayna wa amsal-mulku lillah, wal-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illallah, wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-hamdu, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir: We have reached the evening; all rule belongs to Allah, all praise is His, none deserves worship but Him alone, and He has power over all things.

Evening duas are the ones parents tell me they forget first. Stick them to Maghrib and they stay.

Before Eating

13. Bismillah: In the name of Allah.

14. Allahumma barik lana fima razaqtana, wa qina 'adhaban-nar: O Allah, bless what You gave us to eat, and save us from the Fire's punishment.

After Eating

15. Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi at'amana wa saqana, wa ja'alana minal-muslimin: All praise is for Allah, who fed us, gave us drink, and made us Muslims.

16. Alhamdu lillahi hamdan kathiran tayyiban mubarakan fih: All praise is for Allah, abundant, pure, and blessed praise.

Leaving Home

17. Bismillahi tawakkaltu 'alallah, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah: In Allah's name, I trust in Allah; no strength or power except with Allah.

18. Allahumma inni a'udhu bika an adilla aw udalla, aw azilla aw uzalla, aw azlima aw uzlama, aw ajhala aw yujhala 'alayy: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from going astray or being led astray, from slipping, and from wronging others or being wronged.

Entering Home

19. Bismillahi walajna, wa bismillahi kharajna, wa 'ala rabbina tawakkalna: In Allah's name we enter and leave, and upon our Lord we rely.

20. Assalamu 'alayna wa 'ala 'ibadillahis-salihin: Peace be upon us and upon Allah's righteous servants.

Entering the Masjid

21. A'udhu billahil-'azim, wa bi wajhihil-karim, wa sultanihil-qadim, minash-shaytanir-rajim: I take refuge with Allah, the Mighty, with His noble Face and His ancient authority, from Satan, the rejected one.

22. Bismillah, was-salatu was-salamu 'ala rasulillah. Allahummaftah li abwaba rahmatik: In Allah's name, and blessings and peace be upon Allah's Messenger. O Allah, open the doors of Your mercy for me.

Leaving the Masjid

23. Bismillah, was-salatu was-salamu 'ala rasulillah. Allahumma inni as'aluka min fadlik: In Allah's name, and blessings and peace be upon Allah's Messenger. O Allah, I ask You from Your bounty.

Before Sleeping

24. Bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya: With Your name, O Allah, I go to sleep and I rise again.

25. Allahumma qini 'adhabaka yawma tab'athu 'ibadak: O Allah, save me from Your punishment on the Day You raise Your servants up.

26. Bismika rabbi wada'tu janbi, wa bika arfa'uh: In Your name, my Lord, I lay my side down, and by You I lift it up again.

Teach children the short one first, then let the longer ones come later. Nobody minds a short dua at bedtime.

Traveling

27. Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. Subhanal-ladhi sakhkhara lana hadha wa ma kunna lahu muqrinin, wa inna ila rabbina lamunqalibun: Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest. Glory be to the One who made this ride easy for us, when we could not have managed it ourselves. To our Lord we shall return.

28. Allahumma hawwin 'alayna safarana hadha, watwi 'anna bu'dah: O Allah, make this trip easy for us, and fold up its distance for us.

For Parents

29. Rabbighfir li wa liwalidayya, warhamhuma kama rabbayani saghira: My Lord, forgive me and my parents, and show them mercy, just as they raised me when I was small.

30. Rabbirhamhuma kama rabbayani saghira: My Lord, show them mercy, just as they raised me when I was small.

In Times of Difficulty

31. La ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu minaz-zalimin: There is no god but You, glory be to You. I have been one of the wrongdoers.

32. Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan, wal-'ajzi wal-kasal, wal-bukhli wal-jubn, wa dala'id-dayn, wa ghalabatir-rijal: O Allah, I seek refuge with You from anxiety and sorrow, from weakness and laziness, from miserliness and cowardice, from the weight of debt, and from being overpowered by others.

33. Hasbunallahu wa ni'mal-wakil: Allah is enough for us, and He is the best One to rely on.

Keep these somewhere you can reach them. A hard day is not the time to go hunting for a book.

Seeking Forgiveness

34. Astaghfirullah: I seek Allah's forgiveness.

35. Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbul-'afwa fa'fu 'anni: O Allah, You are Pardoning, and You love to pardon, so pardon me.

General Daily Duas

36. Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanah, wa fil-akhirati hasanah, wa qina 'adhaban-nar: Our Lord, give us good in this life, and good in the life to come, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.

37. Rabbana la tuzigh qulubana ba'da idh hadaytana, wa hab lana min ladunka rahmah. Innaka antal-wahhab: Our Lord, do not let our hearts turn away after You have guided us. Grant us mercy from Yourself. You are the Great Giver.

38. Rabbana afrigh 'alayna sabran, wa thabbit aqdamana: Our Lord, pour patience over us, and make our feet firm.

39. Rabbana hablana min azwajina wa dhurriyyatina qurrata a'yunin, waj'alna lil-muttaqina imama: Our Lord, give us from our spouses and our children comfort for our eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous.

After the Adhan

40. Allahumma rabba hadhihid-da'watit-tammah, was-salatil-qa'imah, ati Muhammadanil-wasilata wal-fadilah, wab'athhu maqaman mahmudanil-ladhi wa'adtah: O Allah, Lord of this complete call and the prayer that is about to stand, give Muhammad the high rank and excellence, and raise him to the praised station that You promised him.

That last one is a good one to learn as a family, because you hear the adhan every day anyway.

How to Learn Them as a Family

One a week, that is my advice, and it is not a slow pace at all. Say the dua at its moment, daily, until your child says it without a prompt. Then add the next one. That is it.

Kids learn these by ear. Not from a worksheet, from hearing you. So say them out loud, at the table, at the door, at bedtime. Some weeks they will join in straight away. Other weeks they will just listen. Both count.

A fridge chart is the oldest trick and it still works. Tick a dua off when it is said alone, no peeking. And when one slips after a holiday, do not restart the whole list. Bring that one back, at its moment, and move on.

And if pronunciation is the worry, that is what a teacher is for. I teach these myself, one child at a time. Try a free 3-day trial, see how it feels, then decide. No pressure.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are masnoon duas?

Duas from the Sunnah. Words the Prophet ﷺ himself said at set moments of the day. When you say them, you are worshipping the way he taught us to worship.

At what age should children start learning daily duas?

Earlier than most parents expect. Three or four is fine for listening, and toddlers pick up Bismillah just from hearing it at meals. By six to eight, one short dua a week is a comfortable pace.

Do I need to say duas in Arabic, or is English enough?

Arabic is best, because it is the exact wording of the Sunnah. But do not let that stop you. Learn what it means in English first, then build the Arabic on top of the meaning. That order sticks.

Can my child learn these duas in a class with you?

Yes, with me personally. I am M Muddasir Hameed, the founder, and the only teacher here, so every lesson is private and one-on-one. Start with a free 3-day trial, no payment, no obligation. After that, the monthly fee simply depends on how many classes a week your child takes. Lessons are private and at home, comfortable for sisters and young girls, and a parent is welcome to sit in every time.

title: How Long Does It Take to Memorize the Entire Quran?
metaDescription: How long to memorize Quran? Explore realistic Hifz timelines for kids and adults, the math behind daily sabaq, and sample 2-year, 3-year, and 5-year plans.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
A mother asked me this in her son's very first trial lesson. "Ustad, how long will it take him to memorize the whole Quran?" I hear some version of that question almost every week, from parents and from adults starting for themselves. So here is my straight answer, the one I give in class. Most students take between two and five years. Where you land in that range depends on something very simple: how much you memorize each day, and whether you revise it properly afterwards.

A full-time student can be done in about two years. A child who goes to school, or an adult who works, usually needs three to five years part-time. That is normal. It is not slow, it is not a failure, it is just what real life allows. In this article I want to show you the actual numbers behind those timelines, what a week of Hifz really looks like, and the one habit that decides whether memorization sticks or slips away.

Allah says in the Quran:

وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا

"And recite the Quran with measured recitation." (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4)

I come back to that verse with every new student. Measured. Not rushed, not raced. Hifz rewards the student who goes slowly and correctly far more than the one who piles up pages and loses half of them a month later.

So, How Long, Really?

Let me give you the picture in plain terms. A full-time Hifz student, memorizing about a page a day, finishes in roughly two years. A dedicated part-time student, half a page a day, takes around three to four years. A school child or a working adult, learning a few lines a day, is looking at four to five years. And someone who can only study at weekends, about a page a week, will take seven years or more.

None of these are promises. They are what I have seen, again and again, when a student keeps a steady pace. Your own timeline will move with three things: how much new lesson you take each day, how seriously you revise, and how consistent you are when life gets busy. A teacher who hears you every single day, as I do with my own students, helps you pick a pace you can honestly keep, instead of one that sounds impressive in week one and collapses by week six.

The Maths Behind It: 604 Pages

The standard Madinah Mushaf has 604 pages, split into 30 Juz. Every day of Hifz has three parts, and students have used the same three names for generations. Sabaq is the new lesson, the fresh verses you memorize that day. Sabqi is revision of what you learned recently, usually the last seven days of Sabaq. Manzil is revision of the older portion, cycling through everything you have covered so far.

Now the division is simple, and I like doing it out loud with students because it removes the mystery. One page of new Sabaq a day means 604 days, about 20 months, and once revision cycles are added on top, that is roughly two years. Half a page a day works out to around three to three and a half years. A quarter page, about four lines a day, comes to roughly five years.

But here is the catch nobody tells you at the start. Real calendar time always runs longer than the division says. Why? Because Manzil grows. By the time you reach Juz 20, you are carrying 19 Juz of revision behind you. That is the part people underestimate. Memorizing is only the first half of Hifz. Keeping it is the second half, and it is the harder one.

Who Finishes When: Kids, Adults, and Weekend Learners

Children aged 7 to 12 in full-time programs often memorize a page a day and finish in about two years. Their memories are flexible, they have few other responsibilities, and the hours are there. But it only works when three things line up: the child wants to be there, the lessons stay engaging, and someone at home supports revision. Take one of those away and even a full-time program stalls.

Most children in the UK, USA, Canada, and Australia go to regular school, so Hifz has to fit into 30 to 60 minutes a day. At half a page a day, that means three to four years. In my experience this is the most common path for families abroad, and it has a quiet advantage people miss. The child usually finishes in the early teens with strong retention, because the slower pace leaves real room for revision. Slower is not weaker here. Often it is stronger.

Adults typically manage a quarter to half a page a day, so three to five years. They have something children do not, though. They know exactly why they are doing it, and that reason carries them through the flat weeks when motivation dips. They also connect verses to their meanings, which anchors memory better than most people expect. And let me say this clearly, because adults ask me all the time: you are never too old. Students in their 40s, 50s, and beyond complete the Quran every single year.

Then there are the weekend-only learners. Seven years or more, maybe. I would never call that a failure, not for a second. Every verse memorized is a treasure kept. The goal just changes, from speed to steady accumulation, one weekend at a time.

What Actually Speeds You Up, and What Slows You Down

Daily consistency beats everything else. Thirty focused minutes every day will beat three hours once a week, and it is not even close. A fixed routine helps for the same reason. When you memorize at the same time each day, Hifz stops being a negotiation with yourself and becomes a habit, like brushing your teeth.

Understanding what you memorize matters more than people think. Reading the translation of each Sabaq gives you meaning anchors, and meaning holds memory in place far better than sound alone. So does reciting to a teacher every day, because small errors get caught before they settle in for good. And Tajweed from day one, not later. Fixing pronunciation afterwards means re-memorizing, doing the work twice.

On the other side, skipping revision is the biggest killer. New Sabaq without Manzil is like pouring water into a leaking bucket. Irregular schedules do similar damage, because long gaps force you to re-memorize portions that had already faded. Taking on too much new lesson is another trap. More than you can revise just builds a backlog of weak memorization. And memorizing alone, with nobody listening, drains motivation fast. Errors go unnoticed, and nobody is there to say, well done, keep going.

Three Sample Plans You Can Actually Follow

The two-year plan is the full-time pace. One full page of Sabaq a day, about 15 lines, Sabqi from the last 7 days, and a full Juz of Manzil on rotation. It needs three to four hours a day, so it suits dedicated full-time students, gap-year students, and adults with open schedules. Rough milestones: Juz 10 by month 8, Juz 20 by month 15, completion around month 20 to 24.

The three-year plan is dedicated part-time. Half a page of Sabaq, 7 to 8 lines, Sabqi from the last 7 days, and Manzil building from half a Juz to a full Juz. Daily time is one and a half to two hours. It suits school-going children with daily classes and committed adults. Milestones run about like this: Juz 10 around month 14, Juz 20 around month 26, completion around month 34 to 38.

The five-year plan is the steady one, and honestly, it is the one most busy families end up loving. A quarter page of Sabaq, 3 to 5 lines, Sabqi from last week's portion, and a quarter Juz of Manzil on rotation, growing gradually. Forty-five to sixty minutes a day. It suits working adults, busy mothers, and young children starting early. Juz 6 by the end of year 1, Juz 12 by mid-year 3, completion in year 5.

Whichever plan you pick, build buffer months into it. Ramadan, exams, travel, illness, life happens. A plan with breathing room is a plan you will actually finish. A plan with no slack is a plan that breaks at the first disruption.

Why Revision Matters More Than New Lessons

Ask any Hafiz what the hardest part was, and most will say retaining, not memorizing. The Prophet ﷺ compared the Quran to a camel: hold its rope and it stays, let go and it escapes. (Sahih al-Bukhari 5033, Sahih Muslim 791)

So what does good revision look like in practice? Every day, recite the last 7 days of Sabaq from memory to your teacher or a study partner, that is your Sabqi. For Manzil, divide everything you have memorized into a rotation, a few pages a day early on, working up to about a Juz a day by Juz 20. Once a month, test yourself: recite a full Juz from memory without looking, and write down the weak spots. And use your Salah. Reciting memorized portions in prayer cements Hifz like nothing else, because you are using the Quran where it belongs.

One golden rule covers all of it, and I repeat it until my students are tired of hearing it. Never take new Sabaq at the cost of Manzil. If revision slips, cut the new lesson down until revision is solid again. It feels like going backwards. It is actually how you move forwards.

Two years or five, childhood or adulthood, full-time or fitted between work and family, the timeline matters far less than the decision to begin. Every Hafiz once stood exactly where you stand now, wondering how long it would take, and started with one verse, then one page, then one Juz. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari 5027) This journey is not a race against the calendar. It is a relationship with the words of Allah that deepens every day you show up. Take the first step today, and book your free 3-day trial class at Noor E Quran Institute.

I will, personally. I am M Muddasir Hameed, founder of Noor E Quran Institute and its only teacher. Every Hifz lesson is private and one-on-one, so your child learns with the same teacher every time, and you always know exactly who is teaching them.
