Yes. Lessons are private, one-on-one, and at home, so you learn somewhere familiar and comfortable. A parent or guardian may sit in on every lesson, the setting respects Islamic etiquette, and any concern comes straight to me.

title: Online vs Mosque Quran Classes: Which Is Better?
metaDescription: Comparing online vs mosque Quran classes for your child? Explore costs, flexibility, teacher quality, and community in this balanced decision guide for parents.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
If you are a parent in the UK, the USA, Canada or Australia, this question has probably come up at home more than once. The local mosque runs Quran classes for children, and online academies offer live one to one lessons from your own living room. So which one is actually better for your child?

Let me be straight with you. There is no single winner here. Both routes have real strengths, and both have real limits. What works for one family can fall flat for another, because it comes down to where you live, how your week looks, how your child learns best, and what matters most to you as a parent. This guide lays both options out side by side, honestly, so you can make the call with a clear head.

What Each Option Really Looks Like

Mosque classes, the madrasa or maktab most of us grew up with, mean your child goes to the local mosque a few evenings a week. Children sit in a group with a teacher, work through Qaida and then the Quran, pick up some Islamic studies along the way, and spend time with other Muslim children from the neighbourhood.

Online classes work differently. Your child joins a live video lesson, one to one, at a time that fits your family. The course runs in order, from Noorani Qaida through Tajweed and into Hifz, and parents get regular updates on how their child is doing. No hall, no commute, just the lesson itself.

Below, I compare the two on the seven points parents usually ask me about first.

A Verse to Keep in Mind

Before the comparison, one verse is worth holding on to, because it reminds us what this effort is really about:

وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ

"And We have certainly made the Quran easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?" (Surah Al-Qamar, 54:17)

The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027) Whichever route you pick, the goal stays the same, that your child learns the Book of Allah properly, with love for it, and keeps that connection as they grow.

Commute and Time

This is often where the decision starts, and for plenty of families it is where it ends too. Mosque classes mean someone has to drive the child there and back, two to five evenings a week, in rain, cold and dark winter evenings. If the mosque is twenty or thirty minutes away, you can easily lose more than an hour a day to driving and waiting around.

Online, that whole trip disappears. Your child sits down at lesson time and the learning starts straight away. The hour you save can go to homework, family time, or simply rest. And if you have two or three children, the saving stacks up fast. For families who live far from a mosque, or who are juggling several children, this point alone often settles it.

Edge: online, especially when distance or several children are in the picture.

Scheduling Flexibility

Mosque timetables are fixed. They usually run on weekday evenings or weekend mornings, and that is that. If you are travelling, your child is unwell, or school throws up a clash, the lesson is gone, with no simple way to catch it up.

Online lessons bend around your week instead. Morning, evening or weekend, you pick the slot, and most academies will move a lesson if you give them notice. A lesson can even happen from a grandparent's house during the holidays, just as easily as from home. Families with shifting schedules, shift work, or frequent travel tend to feel this difference the most.

Edge: online, for families whose weeks rarely look the same twice.

Teacher Quality and Choice

A good local mosque teacher who knows your child by name is a blessing, and many communities are fortunate to have dedicated, qualified mu'allims who give years of their lives to this work. That should be said plainly, and with respect.

Still, honesty matters here too. With a mosque class, you generally take whoever is available locally. That teacher might be superb, or just adequate. You seldom get a real choice, and in some mosques a single part time volunteer is left managing a large group.

Online, the pool is wider in principle, and you can ask harder questions before you commit: what are the teacher's qualifications, how is progress reported, and what happens if the fit is not right? At Noor E Quran Institute, to be clear about our own setup, there is no large roster to choose from. M Muddasir Hameed, the founder, teaches every lesson himself, one to one, so you always know exactly who is teaching your child. That is a different kind of accountability from a group class, and for many parents it is the deciding factor.

Edge: it depends. A superb local teacher will beat an average online teacher any day. But online learning can give you clearer information, regular reporting, and a teacher you can actually hold to account.

One to One Attention or a Group Setting

Most mosque classes are group classes, often fifteen to thirty children with one teacher. In a two hour session, your child might get five or ten minutes of actual recitation, while the rest of the time goes to waiting, listening to others, or drifting off. No teacher, however good, can tailor a lesson to every child in a room that size.

A one to one online lesson turns that around. For the whole session, the teacher's attention is on your child alone. A mistake gets picked up at once, the pace moves at your child's speed, and nothing gets glossed over. Over the same thirty minutes, your child can easily get five times as much active recitation as they would in a group. If steady progress matters to you, this is a hard point to ignore.

Edge: online, clearly, when you measure progress per hour of teaching.

Social Life and Community

Here the mosque has something a screen simply cannot copy. Mosque classes give children real friendships with Muslim peers, a sense of belonging to the local ummah, and a physical link to the house of Allah. For Muslim children growing up as a minority in the West, that sense of identity and belonging carries a weight that goes far beyond the lesson itself.

Online lessons, by their nature, are solitary. Some academies run group events or competitions, and those help, but they are not the same as playing with madrasa friends after class. A child who learns only online may recite beautifully yet feel cut off from the Muslim community around them. That is a genuine cost, and parents should weigh it seriously.

Edge: mosque. This is the one factor online learning cannot truly replace, and it matters a great deal.

Cost

On pure price, mosque classes usually win. Many are free, or ask for a small monthly donation, commonly £20 to £50 per child per month in the UK, because they run as a community service.

Online classes cost more, because you are paying for a teacher's undivided time. Typical packages run from around £30 to £80 or more per month, depending on how many lessons a week you book. For three children, that is a real line in the family budget, and I would not pretend otherwise.

Even so, compare like with like. A mosque fee buys group teaching with limited individual attention. An online fee buys dedicated one to one teaching with progress reports. Once you add the hidden costs of mosque classes, fuel, parking, and your own time, the gap often looks smaller than it did at first glance.

Edge: mosque on price alone, but think about what each pound actually buys you.

Safety and Supervision

A mosque is a public, communal space, and that brings its own reassurance, although how closely children are supervised can vary a lot, and formal background checks for teachers are not always the norm.

Online lessons happen in your home. You can hear the lesson from the next room, you know exactly what is being taught, and there is no journey to worry about. For parents of younger children, that visibility is a real comfort. Lessons at Noor E Quran Institute are private one to one sessions, so a parent can sit nearby or listen in, and there is no mixed group setting to navigate.

Edge: online, for parental oversight, although a well run mosque is also a safe place for children.

Which Fits Your Family? A Simple Framework

There is no universal answer, so use this as a starting point instead:

The mosque is probably the better main choice if:

  • You live close to a mosque with a strong madrasa and a teacher you already trust.
  • Your child is social and comes alive in a group of friends.
  • Community belonging and attachment to the mosque matter most to you right now.
  • Money is tight and the mosque option is free or very cheap.
  • Your week fits the mosque's fixed timetable without a struggle.

Online classes are probably the better main choice if:

  • The nearest good madrasa is far away, or local classes are weak or overcrowded.
  • Your child needs individual attention, whether shy, struggling, ahead of their peers, or easily distracted.
  • Your schedule is irregular, or you travel a lot.
  • You want to know exactly who teaches your child, and to follow their progress closely.
  • You want lessons your child can join from home, with a parent able to listen in.

Consider combining both if:

  • You want the best of both worlds: online one to one lessons two or three times a week for steady progress, plus weekend mosque attendance for community. The teacher handles the personal learning, and the mosque gives your child belonging.

Age plays a part too. Very young beginners, around four to six, often do better with the focused pace of a one to one online lesson, while older children who already read well may gain the most from the mosque's community life.

What Matters Most in the End

Whichever route you choose, the format comes second to three things: a qualified, caring teacher, your child's consistency, and your own involvement. Sit with them for ten minutes a day and go over what they learned. That small daily habit will do more for their progress than any timetable or platform ever could.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who teaches my child at Noor E Quran Institute?

M Muddasir Hameed, the founder, teaches every lesson himself, one to one. There is no rotating roster, so you always know who is teaching your child, and progress is tracked lesson by lesson.

How much do online Quran classes cost each month?

It depends on how many lessons you book each week. Packages at Noor E Quran Institute generally run from around £30 to £80 or more per month, and the fee covers dedicated one to one teaching with regular progress reports to parents.

How does the free 3-day trial work?

You can book a free 3-day trial class to see how a lesson feels before you commit. Your child meets the teacher, tries a real lesson, and you can decide afterwards whether the pace and style suit your family.

Are online lessons comfortable and private for sisters and daughters?

Yes. Lessons are private one to one sessions from your own home, with no mixed group setting. A parent can sit nearby or listen in, and the lesson stays focused on your child's learning in a comfortable, supervised setting.

Conclusion

Mosque classes give you community, affordability and tradition. Online classes give you personal attention, flexibility and a teacher you can follow closely. The wise question is not which one is better in the abstract, but which one is better for your child, right now. Many families find that combining the two, online lessons for learning and the mosque for community, gives their child the complete package. If you would like to see how personalised online learning could work for your family, book a free 3-day trial class at Noor E Quran Institute.

title: Online Quran Teacher: How to Choose the Best for Your Child
metaDescription: A parent's guide to choosing the best online Quran teacher: qualifications like Ijazah and Hifz, trial class checklist, red flags, and questions to ask.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
If you ask me what parents worry about most, it is not the price. It is not the timetable either. It is the teacher. Who is this person, will my child like them, and how do I even tell if they are good? I get that question constantly, and honestly, it is the right question to start with. A child who likes their teacher practises without a row. A child who dreads the lesson will suddenly have a headache every week. So start here, not with the website design.

Here is how I talk parents through it, whether their child ends up with me or with someone else. No jargon, just what to look for.

Why the Teacher Matters More Than the Academy

An academy handles the booking, the platform, the plan on paper. It does not teach. The teacher does. Lesson by lesson. One correction at a time.

Think it through for a second. A letter comes out wrong, who hears it? The teacher. A child goes quiet because they feel embarrassed, who spots that? Again, the teacher, assuming they are actually paying attention. That is why this relationship carries so much weight, more, I would argue, than in maths or English.

Recitation is personal, for one thing. Scare a child and they stop trying, simple as that. Make them feel safe and they will have another go, even after three mistakes in a row. Then there is the time involved. This is not a term's work, it is years. Nobody stays with a teacher they dislike for years. And then, above all, this is the Quran. It deserves a teacher who is not rushed, not careless, and who treats your child with proper respect.

So ignore the glossy homepage for a minute. Ask: who will sit with my child, week after week? Judge that person.

Qualifications to Check, in Order

Not all certificates are worth the same. Some carry real weight, others hardly any. If I am being honest about how I rank them, it looks like this.

1. Ijazah, the gold standard

An Ijazah is not something you pick up over a weekend. A qualified scholar only grants it once a student has recited the entire Quran to them, properly, with Tajweed. Think of it as a licence to teach, one that links a teacher, through their own teachers, right back to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Someone claims to hold one? Ask to see it. A genuine teacher will not take offence, in my experience they are usually glad you checked.

2. Hifz, memorisation of the whole Quran

A Hafiz knows the entire Quran by heart. That helps in ways parents do not always realise. They catch mistakes a non-Hafiz might miss, they recite without fumbling, and they show your child, just by being there, what memorisation actually looks like. For a Hifz student, I would call this close to essential.

3. Formal Islamic education

Did they study at a recognised madrasa or university? Do they actually understand Tajweed and Qiraat, or can they only repeat rules? There is a difference, and children feel it fast. A teacher who knows why a letter sounds the way it does can explain it in ten seconds. A teacher who does not will just say "repeat" until the child gives up.

4. Experience teaching children

This one gets overlooked, and it should not. Teaching an adult is one skill. Teaching a five year old on a video call is another job completely. Ask directly: how long have you taught children online? A brilliant reciter with no experience of a restless six year old can struggle badly, while a less famous teacher who knows children will have that same child laughing and learning in ten minutes.

5. Language your child understands

Simple, but crucial. Your child needs a teacher who speaks their language properly, usually English for families in the UK, USA, Canada, and Australia, on top of Arabic. One clear explanation beats twenty blind repetitions. Every time.

The Trial Class: What to Actually Watch For

One plea: never enrol without a trial. And when you do get one, do not just go through the motions. That half hour is your only real chance to watch the actual teacher with your actual child, before any money is involved.

Before the class, did anyone confirm the time? Send the login details? Ask what level your child is at, and what you are hoping for? These little things tell you a lot about how organised the teaching will be.

During the class, watch more than you listen. Does the teacher greet your child properly, spend a minute warming up, or dive straight into corrections? Have they bothered to check what level your child is at? How is their own recitation, because beautiful, correct recitation is non-negotiable, however friendly they seem. When a mistake happens, is it put right gently, right there and then, not shouted about, and not just left? Do they explain the reason, something like "this letter comes from the throat", or is it just "again, again" on repeat? Is your child actually engaged, or have they gone quiet? And at the end, is there encouragement, and a clear bit of homework?

Afterwards, just ask your child: did you like them, want to carry on with them? Kids are terrible at faking that answer. A real, enthusiastic yes beats any brochure you will ever read.

Red Flags: When to Walk Away

Your gut is useful here, genuinely. Spot any of this, and walk away, or ask for someone different.

Weak recitation from the teacher themselves. If they mispronounce letters or rush through verses, they cannot teach your child properly. That is the biggest red flag there is, full stop.

No patience. Shouting, shaming, a teacher visibly frustrated with a child. Never acceptable, no matter how many certificates are on the wall.

No trial offered. An academy that wants your money before your child has met the teacher is selling, not teaching.

Vague answers about qualifications. "Our teachers are all qualified" tells you nothing. You want names, specifics, Ijazah, Hifz, years, where they studied.

A teacher who does not want a parent nearby. A good teacher welcomes it.

No plan, no progress reports. If nobody can say what your child will learn this term, they are making it up as they go.

And pressure. Countdown timers, "only one slot left", that sort of thing. That is sales, not education.

Male or Female Teacher: What Should You Choose?

For little ones, under about seven, honestly, either works. What matters is warmth and patience, not gender.

For older daughters, many families prefer a female teacher. Same for mothers and sisters learning themselves, a female teacher often feels more comfortable, and that preference is completely understandable.

For sons, plenty of families are happy with either, though some like a male teacher as a role model for older boys.

Whatever you choose, keep the standard the same: qualifications, experience with children, a trial your child enjoys. One thing I should be clear about here. At Noor E Quran Institute, I teach every student myself, so the trial is with me, the actual teacher, not a stand-in. Lessons are private, one-on-one, at home, and a parent can sit in on every class, which keeps things comfortable for sisters and young girls.

Questions to Ask Before You Enrol

Do not feel shy about asking these. A good teacher expects them.

  1. What are your qualifications: Ijazah, Hifz, formal Islamic education?
  2. How long have you taught children online, specifically?
  3. Can we trial with the actual teacher who will teach my child?
  4. Will my child keep the same teacher long-term?
  5. What is the curriculum, and how will I get progress reports?
  6. What happens if we miss a class, is there a makeup policy?
  7. What is the exact monthly fee, and is there a sibling discount?
  8. Who do I contact if I ever have a concern?

If they answer all eight patiently, that tells you something. If they dodge, well, that tells you something too.

Your Role After Choosing

The teacher cannot do this alone. Parents have a part too, and it is simpler than people think.

Protect the schedule. Treat class time like school time, not optional. Sit in now and then, read the progress reports, but let the teacher teach. And if something feels off, progress slowing, your child unhappy, say so early. Do not wait three months hoping it sorts itself out. At home, ten minutes of revision a day does more than you would believe. The teacher plants, you water. That is how it grows.

Allah says in the Quran:

وَقُل رَّبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا

"And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge." (Quran, Taha 20:114)

I think about that verse whenever a parent asks me this question. Because choosing a teacher is not really about hiring a tutor. It is about asking Allah to increase your child in knowledge, and then picking the person who will carry that knowledge to them, one lesson at a time.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari 5027) Find a teacher who lives that, not just quotes it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who will teach my child at Noor E Quran Institute?

I will, personally. I am M Muddasir Hameed, founder of Noor E Quran Institute and its only teacher. Every lesson is private and one-on-one, so your child learns with the same teacher every time, and you always know exactly who is teaching them.

How does the free 3-day trial work?

Three full one-on-one lessons, free, with no payment and no obligation. It is genuine teaching, not a sales call, and it shows me your child's level, so the first paid lesson starts exactly where it should.

How much do online Quran classes cost each month?

The monthly fee depends on how many classes your child takes each week. Current plans are on the packages page, and sibling discounts are available. Ask for the exact fee for your schedule before you enrol, and be wary of any academy that will not state it plainly.

Is it private and comfortable for my daughter or for sisters learning?

Yes. Lessons are private, one-on-one, and at home, so your daughter learns somewhere familiar and comfortable. A parent or guardian may sit in on every lesson, and any concern comes straight to me.

Conclusion

So it comes down to a handful of honest checks, nothing fancy. Qualifications you can verify. Experience with children, not just adults. A trial your child enjoys. Straight answers instead of dodging. Plus your own instinct, which honestly counts for more than most guides admit. You will know when you have found the right teacher, your child will head to the lesson willingly instead of dragging their feet. Book your free 3-day trial class at Noor E Quran Institute, and judge it by how your child responds to a teacher who has time for them alone.

title: Quran Memorization Techniques: Sabaq, Sabqi & Manzil
metaDescription: Learn the traditional quran memorization techniques of Sabaq, Sabqi, and Manzil — the time-tested Hifz system for memorizing the Quran systematically.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
People ask me this all the time. How does someone actually memorise the whole Quran? All of it? My answer is usually disappointing at first, because there is no secret. No trick. Just a routine, repeated daily, for years, until it becomes part of life. In traditional teaching that routine has three names. Sabaq. Sabqi. Manzil.

That is it, really. Sabaq is today's new lesson. Sabqi is going back over the last few days. Manzil is the long revision, the old portions, cycled round again and again. Together they form a complete quran hifz program, and the point is not just to get the Quran memorised. It is to keep it. For life. If you are a parent weighing up Hifz for your child, or an adult who has quietly wanted to start for years, start here. Understand these three first.

Allah says:

وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ

"And We have certainly made the Quran easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?" (Surah Al-Qamar, 54:17)

Easy does not mean no effort. It means the path is open. This is the path teachers have used for centuries.

Not Cramming. Something Else Entirely.

School taught most of us to cram. Learn it tonight, pass tomorrow, forget it next week. Hifz is the opposite of that. You are not trying to know a page for a day. You are trying to be able to recite any verse, any time, without stopping to search for it in your head.

So you meet the same verses at three distances. New today. Recent this week. Old, over months and years. Drop one distance, and things start to slip. I explain it to parents like building a wall. Sabaq lays new bricks. Sabqi checks yesterday's bricks are straight. Manzil walks the whole wall, week after week, checking for cracks. It is a simple picture. It works.

Sabaq: Today's New Bit

Sabaq means lesson, plain and simple. The fresh portion you memorise each day. The leading edge of the journey.

How Much, Though?

Here is where parents often get it wrong, with the best intentions. More is not better. The rule I use: take only what you can hold perfectly. A shaky page is not progress. It is a repair job you have just created for yourself.

Children around five to ten usually do half a page to a page a day. Older students, adults, maybe one or two pages. Full-time students, more again. But honestly, the number is secondary. One perfect page beats five wobbly ones. Every time.

A teacher has to judge this, day by day. Too much Sabaq and a child dreads the lesson. Too little and the whole journey stretches out pointlessly. Getting that balance right, that is half the skill.

Inside a Sabaq Lesson

Listen first. The teacher recites the new portion properly, Tajweed included, so it lands in the ear before the mouth has a go. Then verse by verse. Repeat one verse till it flows, link it to the next, keep going till the portion holds together. Then the part students both dread and need: recite it all from memory, to the teacher, mistakes fixed there and then. Not left to settle overnight.

That daily moment matters. You know you will have to recite tomorrow, so you concentrate today in a way self-study rarely forces. The Prophet ﷺ taught that the best among people are those who learn the Quran and teach it, as reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027. That daily sitting, learning and being corrected, keeps the effort honest.

Sabqi: The Last Seven Days, Every Day

Sabqi is what came just before. In practice, the last seven days of Sabaq, recited to the teacher daily. No skipping.

Why seven days? Because fresh memory lies to you. A verse from yesterday feels solid today. Leave it alone for a week and it can fall apart. I have watched this happen so many times. Sabqi grabs the memory while it is fresh and works it daily, until it moves into long-term memory. Each new portion gets revised roughly seven times in that first week, exactly when forgetting is most likely to hit.

Students who stick with Sabqi say the same thing eventually. It locks in. One day it just clicks. Students who skip it, even briefly, find themselves relearning pages they thought were done. Unflashy work. But this is where Hifz is won or lost, quietly.

Manzil: The Long Cycle

Manzil means a stage on a journey, a stopping place. For Hifz it means revising everything old, everything beyond the Sabqi window.

You divide all you have memorised into a rotating cycle, one section a day. The usual aim: finish the whole cycle once a week. A student with ten juz memorised revises about a juz and a half daily in Manzil. As the total grows, the daily Manzil grows too, until a Hafiz is revising four or five juz a day. Sounds like a lot, and it is. But it builds gradually, over years.

Without Manzil, even well-learned portions fade within months. With a weekly cycle kept up for years, verses become part of a person. You meet elderly Huffaz who can recite any page flawlessly, decades later, and this is why. Do it out loud, by the way, to a listener. Silent reading hides hesitations. Speaking brings them out, which is precisely what you want.

What a Day Actually Looks Like

Take a school-age child in a structured program. Morning, before school, thirty to forty-five minutes. Recite yesterday's Sabaq plus Sabqi to the teacher, start today's Sabaq. Later, afternoon or evening, another thirty to forty-five minutes. Finish today's Sabaq, do the day's Manzil aloud, glance back over the last three days.

Adults do the same thing, smaller. Half a page of Sabaq, a short Sabqi, a modest Manzil. The Quran still gets completed, just over several years rather than two or three. The system fits your pace. It does not fit a day with a part missing altogether.

Why a Teacher Needs to Hear You Daily

Could you do it alone? Maybe, in theory. I have rarely seen it last in practice. A teacher is not just listening. He adjusts the pace, easing Sabaq back when retention is weak, instead of letting weak pages stack up. He catches problems within a day, because he hears Sabaq and Sabqi daily. He corrects Tajweed from the very first recitation, since a mistake memorised is learned twice over. He tests over larger portions weekly and monthly, checking Manzil is genuinely holding. And he knows when a student needs encouragement, a lighter day, or a new challenge.

Alone, small errors creep in and motivation fades, slowly, without you noticing. In a supervised quran memorization program, every part gets witnessed and guided, day after day.

A Note for Parents at Home

You matter here, even if you are not a Hafiz. Guard the time like school time, because Hifz depends on daily consistency. Listen to Manzil when you can. You only need to follow in the mushaf while your child recites, no correcting required.

Mark each juz finished. Celebrate it. Those good memories last a lifetime. When progress stalls, and it will at times, praise effort, not just results. Make dua together. Remind your child this is for Allah, and ask Him to make it easy and lasting.

If older portions weaken, do not worry. That is normal. It is what Manzil exists to fix. The teacher will usually cut back new Sabaq for a bit and set focused revision until things are strong again. Completely standard, not a failure.

And Tajweed before Hifz? Not required. Tajweed is learned alongside, verse by verse, as each new portion comes. Noorani Qaida plus basic Nazra reading is enough to begin.

Trust the system. Give it time. Millions of Huffaz never looked for shortcuts. They turned up daily, took a manageable Sabaq, revised Sabqi, cycled Manzil, and let a teacher guide them. That way, memorisation does not just fill the mind. It settles in the heart, for life.

Begin with personal guidance and a free trial. Book your free 3-day trial class at Noor E Quran Institute.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to complete Hifz with Sabaq, Sabqi, and Manzil?

With one page of Sabaq daily, the full Quran takes about two to three years including revision. Full-time children often finish in two to four years, while part-time adults typically take four to seven years. Retention matters more than speed, and a supervised system produces Hifz that lasts.

How much do online Hifz classes cost, and is there a free trial?

Fees depend on the number of classes per week and are shared clearly before you enrol, with no hidden charges. Every new student can start with a free 3-day trial, three full classes, so you can see the teaching and the Sabaq, Sabqi, Manzil routine before paying anything.

Who teaches the Hifz classes?

Every lesson is taught personally by the founder himself, M Muddasir Hameed, in a private one-on-one class. There are no rotating tutors and no substitutes, so your child learns from the same teacher every day.

Are online Hifz classes comfortable and private for sisters and daughters?

Yes. Classes are private one-on-one sessions in a comfortable setting that respects Islamic etiquette for sisters and young girls. Parents are welcome to sit nearby, and lesson times can be set to suit your family's timezone in the UK, USA, Canada, or Australia.

title: Improve Your Quran Recitation: 7 Practical Tips
metaDescription: Discover how to improve Quran recitation with 7 practical tips: makharij, pacing, listening, recording, revision, breath control, and teacher feedback today.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Want to recite better? Focus on seven practical habits and practise them daily: correct makharij, slower reading, listening to master reciters, recording yourself, a proper revision loop, controlled breathing, and regular teacher feedback. That is the whole method. No secret, no special talent required, just a routine you actually keep.

Allah describes the standard Himself: وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا, "and recite the Quran with measured, deliberate recitation" (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4). Tartil is slow, clear, deliberate reading, the opposite of racing to the end of a page. Hold your own recitation against that word and you will usually know at once what needs work.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it" (Sahih al-Bukhari 5027). That hadith is why this guide ends with a teacher, not with a technique. Learning the Quran has always involved someone listening to you and correcting you.

Tip 1: Fix the Letters at Their Source

A letter sounds right only when it comes from its right place, its makhraj. Throat, tongue, lips, nasal passage, mouth cavity: five areas, and every letter belongs to one of them. Get the place wrong and the sound is wrong, and occasionally the meaning follows it.

You probably already know which pairs catch you out. For most learners it is س and ص, or ت and ط, or the ذ, ز, ظ set, or ح slipping into ه. Practise those pairs deliberately, not the letters you already say well. Say each one with fatha, dammah, and kasrah, and notice, really notice, what your tongue and lips are doing.

A teacher's makharij check early on is worth more than months of solo drilling, because a trained ear spots in minutes what you might practise wrongly for a year. Give this two or three weeks before you chase anything else. It is the foundation, and foundations are boring until you see what they hold up.

Tip 2: Slow Is a Skill, Not a Step Back

Most learners read too fast, full stop. Letters blur together, madd gets shortened, waqf signs get ignored. The recitation sounds busy rather than beautiful, and busy is not the same as fluent.

Here is a two week experiment: read at half speed, pointer under each word, one verse at a time. After each verse, check only two things. Full madd? Right waqf? It will feel strange, even frustrating, at first. Good. That friction means you are actually noticing your reading for once.

Pick a page you know, time it, then read it again taking roughly a fifth longer and see how much more you catch. Speed returns later, on its own, once slow reading is comfortable. The other way round, speed first and accuracy later, rarely works.

Tip 3: Let Your Ear Do the Teaching

Listening is not passive time. It is how your brain learns what correct recitation sounds like, so that your tongue has a target to aim at. Without it, you are practising in the dark.

Start with one reciter who reads slowly and clearly. Mishary Alafasy and Saad Al-Ghamdi are safe choices for learners. Listen to the surah you are working on, mushaf open, and repeat each verse after the reciter, the shadowing habit. Ten to fifteen minutes a day of this, with full attention, does more than an hour of background listening.

Switch reciters monthly if you want variety. And do not underestimate the motivation side: the more beautiful recitation sounds to you, the more you will want to sit down and practise. Taste drives effort.

Tip 4: Record, Listen, Fix One Thing

Nobody hears themselves the way others hear them. A recording closes that gap, fast, and sometimes uncomfortably. That discomfort is the point. It shows you the exact problem instead of a vague feeling that something is off.

Your phone recorder is enough. One page, or five verses. Listen tomorrow, with fresh ears, and write the mistakes down in plain words: madd shortened here, letter swallowed there, stop in the wrong place, tune flat. Then choose one category for the week. One. Everything at once means nothing gets fixed.

When students of Tajweed bring recordings to lessons, the lesson changes. The teacher stops searching for the problem and starts fixing it, and the student leaves with a clear job for the week. Share yours if you can.

Tip 5: New, Recent, Old, Every Session

Sabaq, sabqi, manzil. New lesson, recent revision, old revision. That three part cycle is how traditional students kept hundreds of pages alive at once, and it still works. The learners who feel stuck are almost always the ones doing only the first part.

Try 15 minutes new, 10 minutes recent, 10 minutes old, in every session. New verses get read at least five times each before you move on. If you memorise, yesterday's portion gets recited to someone at home first, no exceptions, before new material.

Thirty minutes a day, every day, will outperform a heroic three hour weekend session. I have seen it too many times to doubt it. Small and daily wins.

Tip 6: Train the Breath Behind the Voice

A verse cut short by empty lungs loses both meaning and beauty. Breath control sounds like a singer's concern, but for recitation it decides where you may pause and where you may not, and that is a Tajweed matter, not a performance one.

Three slow breaths through the nose before you begin will settle your breathing more than you expect. Mark sensible stopping points in pencil in your mushaf, following the waqf signs, so you are planning your breath instead of discovering its end mid-verse. Sit up straight, because posture and lung capacity are linked. And for a genuinely long verse, stop at an approved waqf point and resume, never in the middle of a phrase that belongs together.

A few weeks of this and your breath span stretches, often sooner than students believe. It is a quiet improvement, but it makes long verses feel possible instead of daunting.

Tip 7: A Teacher's Ear, Week After Week

Self study will take you a long way, and then it will stop, because your own blind spots are, by definition, invisible to you. A teacher sees them at once, names the rule behind them, and keeps you accountable to a plan that changes as you change.

Two or three live sessions a week is plenty. Arrive with your list from your recordings, so the lesson targets real weaknesses. Leave with one correction to work on, one only, and return ready to show it. That loop, repeated weekly, is where most progress actually happens.

Private 1-on-1 lessons give that loop the best conditions, since the entire session is your recitation. At Noor E Quran Institute, the founder, M Muddasir Hameed, teaches every lesson himself, so the same teacher tracks your reading from lesson to lesson. Start with a free 3-day trial class if you want to experience that feedback before deciding anything.

Putting It Together: 35 Minutes a Day

  • Minutes 1 to 5: Deep breaths, then a makharij warm-up on tricky letters with all three harakat.
  • Minutes 5 to 15: New lesson, slow, five repeats a verse, audio first.
  • Minutes 15 to 25: Revision loop, recent pages, then an older page.
  • Minutes 25 to 30: Record two or three verses, listen back, note one fix for tomorrow.
  • Minutes 30 to 35: A beloved surah, read for joy alone.

Lesson days replace the recording slot with the live session. One day a week stays light, listening and joyful reading only. Beautiful recitation is built, not born, and the building happens in these small daily sessions. Record yourself on day one, then again on day thirty, and listen to the two side by side. No advice motivates quite like hearing your own progress.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who will teach me or my child?

M Muddasir Hameed, the founder of Noor E Quran Institute, teaches every lesson himself in private 1-on-1 classes. No teacher rotation, no handovers: the same teacher follows you or your child from the first lesson onward. You can begin with a free 3-day trial class, with no commitment.

How much do online Quran classes cost?

The fee is monthly, and it depends on how many classes per week you choose. We confirm the exact fee with you before enrolment, so nothing comes as a surprise, and the free 3-day trial comes first either way.

Can sisters learn comfortably and privately?

Yes. Every lesson is a private 1-on-1 session from home, so there is no group class and no one else present. Sisters learn in full privacy, family members can sit nearby if they wish, and the founder teaches every student with the same care and respect.

How long does it take to noticeably improve recitation?

Most students notice real improvement within four to six weeks of 30 focused minutes daily plus weekly teacher feedback. Full fluency with proper Tajweed typically takes several months to a year, and that timeline is normal, not a sign of failure.

title: Online Quran Classes for Kids: What Every Parent Should Know
metaDescription: A parent's guide to online Quran classes for kids: how lessons work, safety, scheduling worldwide, trial classes, what to look for, and tracking progress.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Let me answer the question straight, the way I would if you asked me after a lesson. Do online Quran classes for kids actually work? Yes, when three things are right. One teacher who gives your child his full attention. A clear path from the first letter to fluent reading. And a parent who can see what is happening in every single lesson. When those three are in place, a child in London or Toronto or Sydney can learn the Quran properly, even if the nearest madrasa is a forty-minute drive away, or there is no madrasa near you at all.

Before anything about platforms or schedules, one thing matters more, and it is not mine to invent. Allah puts this duty on parents first:

وَأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ بِالصَّلَاةِ وَاصْطَبِرْ عَلَيْهَا ۖ لَا نَسْأَلُكَ رِزْقًا ۖ نَّحْنُ نَرْزُقُكَ ۗ وَالْعَاقِبَةُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ

"And enjoin prayer upon your family, and be steadfast in it. We ask you not for provision; We provide for you, and the best outcome is for the righteous." (Surah Taha, 20:132)

I keep coming back to that verse when parents ask me where to start. The teacher helps. The timetable helps. But the home is where a child's Quran habit takes root or quietly dies. Everything below follows from that.

How a Lesson Actually Looks

Forget the crowded classroom picture. A proper online lesson is small and private: one child, one teacher, one video call. Here is what usually happens, step by step.

Your child logs in at the agreed time, on Zoom or Google Meet, from whatever device you already have at home. We open gently, a short dua, then a quick look back at the last lesson, because a child who revises a little every time forgets a lot less. Then the screen does the heavy lifting. I share the Noorani Qaida page, or the Quran page, or a Tajweed chart, and point at letters as your child reads them out loud.

Then the real work: listen, repeat, correct. I read a sound. Your child copies it. If the makhraj is off, I correct it there and then, not next week, not in a report card. Try getting that in a hall of thirty children. One teacher, thirty voices, and your child's small mistake slides past unnoticed, week after week, until it hardens into a habit.

We finish with a short revision task, five to fifteen minutes, and an encouraging word. That is it. No drama. Young children usually manage 25 to 30 minutes well; older children can go up to an hour. Most families I teach settle on two to five classes a week, fitted around school, not the other way round.

What Do You Need at Home?

Honestly, very little. A device with a camera and microphone, internet that does not keep dropping, and a quiet corner. No software to buy. No textbooks to order. The lesson material comes in digital form, so your child needs nothing you do not already own.

Why So Many Parents Have Switched

I speak to parents every week who tried the local option first, and the reasons they give are strikingly similar.

Attention, for one. In a one-on-one lesson, every minute belongs to your child. Every mistake is heard. Progress is usually much faster than in a group, and parents notice it within weeks, not terms.

Distance stops mattering, too. I have taught children in towns where the nearest qualified teacher was hours away. Online, that problem disappears. A family with no madrasa nearby can still give their child a teacher who knows the work properly.

Then there is the practical side, and parents are frank about it. No commute. Lessons before or after school, on weekends, in your own local time. If you travel, or move country, the classes move with you. And you can sit beside your child and hear every word taught. Nothing happens behind a closed door, and that matters more to parents than any brochure promise.

One more thing parents mention, quietly: control. Because the lesson is private and at home, you decide who sits in, what gets discussed, and whether something needs to change. If it does not suit your family, you say so, directly, to the person teaching your child.

Safety: The Questions You Should Ask

A video call between your child and an adult teacher deserves proper scrutiny. I would rather a parent ask me hard questions than enrol on trust alone. So ask these, of anyone:

  • Can I sit in? For children under about eight, you or another trusted adult should be within earshot of every class. An academy that resists this is telling you something. Listen to it.
  • Who exactly is the teacher? A name, a background, a qualification, and how the academy verified them. Vague answers here are a warning sign, full stop.
  • Which platform? Lessons should run on recognised video platforms such as Zoom or Google Meet. Not an obscure app. Not private messaging.
  • What about recordings? Are lessons recorded, who can view them, how are they stored? You deserve a straight answer, in plain words.
  • Who do I call with a concern? You should reach the founder or management directly, not only the teacher. If there is no such line, ask why.

An honest academy welcomes this list. If one turns evasive, or discourages you from sitting in, walk away. There are better options, and your child deserves one of them.

Choosing an Academy: Six Questions That Tell You Everything

1. Who will actually teach my child?

Ask for a name, not a promise. Does the teacher hold Ijazah, the certification to teach the Quran? Have they studied Tajweed formally? And, crucially, how many years have they spent teaching children? Teaching a six-year-old is a different skill from teaching an adult, and it shows within one lesson. At Noor E Quran Institute, this question has a short answer: I teach every class myself, so you always know exactly who is with your child.

2. Is the trial real?

Here is a simple test. In a real trial, your child studies. In a fake one, you get a sales call with a lesson's name on it. I have heard the second version described to me by parents more times than I can count, and it always ends the same way: a polite conversation, a discount deadline, and no teaching at all. So ask, plainly, what happens in the trial. Ours is three full lessons, free, over three days. Your child reads, I listen, I correct, and by the end you know what the teaching actually feels like. That is the whole point.

3. Is there a real curriculum, or just good intentions?

"What will my child learn, and in what order?" If an academy cannot answer that in one breath, be suspicious. The path should sound like this: Noorani Qaida first, then Nazra, then Tajweed, then Hifz only if and when the child is ready, with milestones you can actually see and a progress report every month. Ask to see a sample report. A serious academy has one ready. A vague one will change the subject.

4. Is the pricing plain?

Fees should be out in the open: monthly cost, classes included, sibling discounts. If an academy will not talk money until you have sat through a long sales conversation, that delay is rarely an accident. It is a tactic. Walk past it.

5. What happens when life happens?

Because it will. Children fall sick the night before a lesson. Families travel. A good academy has a simple answer ready: yes, you can reschedule, and yes, missed classes are credited. If the policy needs three paragraphs and a footnote to explain, it was probably written to protect the academy, not your family.

6. Does one teacher own the progress?

Think about it this way. When five teachers rotate through a child's week, who actually knows that child? Nobody, really. Everyone knows a slice. When one teacher teaches every lesson, that teacher carries the whole picture: the strengths, the weak spots, the pace that works, the days when confidence dips. And you know exactly who to call. That is the model I built Noor E Quran Institute on, and I have not found a reason to change it.

Timezones Without the Headache

London, Toronto, Sydney, Chicago: everyone learns in their own local time. You choose the slot that fits your household, after school, in the evening, at the weekend. The academy bends around you, not the reverse. After-school windows do fill up, so earlier is better, and a reminder before each class helps the routine survive busy weeks. Ask any parent: the routine surviving is half the battle.

What Parents Can Do at Home

I say this in nearly every first lesson, because the lesson alone is never the whole story.

Sit in when you can, especially with younger children. Your presence steadies them. It also says something louder than any lecture: the Quran matters to you, not just to their teacher. Children notice that. They always do.

Revise a little, every day. Five focused minutes beats a heroic hour once a week. I have never seen an exception to this, in all my years of teaching. Small and daily wins, every single time.

Praise effort, not just results. "You worked hard on those letters today" does more for a child than "Why did you get that wrong?" ever will. Children remember the tone of a lesson long after they forget its content.

Never punish slow progress, and never compare siblings. I mean this seriously. Pressure and comparison are the quickest route I know to a child who resents Quran study, and resentment, once it sets in, is miserable to undo.

And let them see you read. Not hear about reading. See it. Read where they can see you, make dua where they can hear you. Children copy what they watch far more than what they are told.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027) A parent who sits beside a child, revises with them, reads in front of them, is already part of that teaching, before any lesson begins.

The Path, From the First Letter to Hifz

Children move at their own pace, but the road is well worn, and it looks like this:

  1. Noorani Qaida (3 to 6 months). Alphabet, pronunciation, joining letters. This stage decides everything that follows, so it is never rushed, no matter how eager anyone is to move on.
  2. Nazra, Quran Reading (6 to 12 months). The whole Quran, read fluently, page by page, with Tajweed woven in as the reading grows stronger.
  3. Tajweed (ongoing). The rules of beautiful, correct recitation, refined a little at a time, never dumped on a child all at once.
  4. Hifz, Memorization (2 to 4 years, optional). Only when the child is ready, and only when the child wants it. A forced Hifz rarely lasts, and a willing one is a different thing entirely.
  5. Islamic Studies and Duas (alongside). Salah, daily duas, stories of the Prophets, everyday manners, learned in small pieces over years.

The trial class doubles as an assessment. I listen to your child read, and place them where they belong, even mid-path. No wasted months repeating what they know. No child thrown into deep water before they can swim.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who will teach my child?

I will, personally. I am M Muddasir Hameed, founder of Noor E Quran Institute and its only teacher. Every lesson is private and one-on-one, so sisters and young girls learn in a comfortable setting that respects Islamic etiquette, and a parent is welcome to sit in on any class.

How does the free 3-day trial work?

Three full one-on-one lessons, free, with no payment and no obligation. It is genuine teaching, not a sales call, and it shows me your child's level, so the first paid lesson starts exactly where it should.

How much do online Quran classes for kids cost?

Good academies generally charge around $30 to $80 USD a month, depending on weekly classes. At Noor E Quran Institute the fee follows your weekly schedule, current plans are on the packages page, and sibling discounts are available.

Is it private and comfortable for my daughter?

Yes. Lessons are private, one-on-one, and at home, so your daughter learns somewhere familiar and comfortable. A parent or guardian may sit in on every lesson, and any concern comes straight to me.

Conclusion

So, the decision. It is one of the most meaningful you will make as a parent, and it need not be complicated. A teacher you know by name. A trial that actually teaches. A path from Qaida to fluent reading that you can see. Pricing stated plainly. And an academy that welcomes you into the virtual classroom instead of merely tolerating you there. The surest way to judge all of it is to try it. Book the free 3-day trial at Noor E Quran Institute, and see for yourself how your child responds to a teacher with time for them alone.

title: What Is Ijazah? Understanding Quran Certification
metaDescription: What is Ijazah? Learn the meaning of Quran Ijazah certification, the Sanad chain to the Prophet ﷺ, its types and requirements, and how to earn Ijazah online.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
Parents ask me about Ijazah more than almost any other qualification. They see the word on a teacher's profile, next to Sanad, and they want to know what it proves. Put simply, an Ijazah is a scholar's written permission. It says: this student has mastered Quran recitation or memorization, and this student may now teach it.

That permission carries weight because it is hard to get. No one earns it in a weekend. A student sits with a teacher for months, sometimes years, recites, gets corrected, recites again, and in the end recites the entire Quran in that teacher's hearing. This guide walks through the meaning of Ijazah, the Sanad behind it, its main types, the work involved, and how preparation looks online today.

What Does Ijazah Actually Mean?

Ijazah (إجازة) is Arabic for permission, or authorization. In Quranic study it means a formal licence from a master scholar. The scholar gives it to a student who has shown full mastery of a subject, usually recitation or memorization of the Quran.

It helps to compare it with a licence to drive. Passing a short course is not enough, and neither is attendance. You prove yourself in practice, again and again, until the person licensing you is sure. With Ijazah, the proof is reciting the whole Quran to your teacher, letter by letter, with every rule in place. The teacher's name goes on that certificate, so the teacher checks carefully. He is vouching for your recitation of Allah's words, and for your readiness to teach them.

Scholars started this system in Islam's early centuries, first for passing on hadith, then for Quranic recitation and other sciences. It is often described as the world's oldest system of formal certification. University degrees came centuries later.

The Sanad: A Chain That Reaches Back to the Prophet

An ordinary certificate stands on its own. An Ijazah does not. It comes with a Sanad (سند), a documented chain of teachers. Your teacher learned from his teacher, who learned from his teacher, and so on, back to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, who received the Quran from Jibreel.

Why does that chain matter? Because the Quran was preserved by people, not only by books. Written copies existed, yes, but alongside them ran a living line of reciters. Each one heard the Quran from a teacher and passed the sound on, pronunciation, rhythm, pauses and all. Fourteen centuries later, that spoken line is still unbroken.

Allah says:

إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ

"Indeed, it is We who sent down the Quran and indeed, We will be its guardian." (Quran 15:9)

The Sanad is one of the human means Allah used to guard His Book.

Types of Ijazah in Quranic Studies

Students usually aim for one of three types, depending on their goal.

Ijazah in Recitation (Tilawah) with Tajweed

The student reads the whole Quran from the mushaf to the teacher, with Tajweed applied throughout. Every slip counts: a wrong Makhraj, the articulation point of a letter, a missed Tajweed rule, a shaky pause. The teacher grants the Ijazah only when the full Quran has been read accurately.

Ijazah in Hifz (Memorization)

Here the student recites the whole Quran from memory, in daily portions, over many weeks. Memory alone is not enough. The recitation must still follow every Tajweed rule. A student can also earn both together, a combined Ijazah in recitation and memorization.

Ijazah in the Qiraat (the Ten Readings)

This is the advanced level. A student who already holds an Ijazah studies the canonical readings, for example Hafs from Asim and Warsh from Nafi, and learns where they differ in pronunciation and wording.

What It Takes to Earn One

Be honest with yourself before you start. Ijazah work is demanding, and the requirements leave little room for shortcuts.

You need solid Tajweed first. Most teachers expect a full Tajweed course behind you, so the rules feel natural before Ijazah work starts. You need fluent, accurate recitation, with correct Makharij and a calm, steady delivery. You need time, several sessions a week, month after month. And above all, you need to recite the entire Quran to your teacher, cover to cover, while he listens and corrects you live. Teachers also look at character and sincerity. You are asking for a licence to teach Allah's Book, after all.

So, how long? If you already recite well and study several times a week, plan on one to three years. Anyone promising it in a few weeks is selling something else. Your teacher must hear the whole Quran from you himself. There is no way around that.

Nor is there one big exam at the end. Instead, you work through the Quran session by session. Passages with mistakes get repeated until they are clean. Near the end, your teacher may retest chosen portions. Then, and only then, comes the written certificate: your name, the type of Ijazah, and the full Sanad back to the Prophet, peace be upon him. Some teachers add a test of Tajweed theory too.

Why Parents Should Care About Ijazah

Four reasons, plainly put. First, accuracy that has been checked. A holder's recitation was examined letter by letter against the transmitted standard. Second, a real licence to teach. Ijazah means permission to teach, so a certified teacher is much less likely to hand your child his own mistakes. Third, openness. A teacher worth trusting will show you his Sanad and qualifications when you ask. Fourth, connection. Your child joins a chain that has carried the Quran for fourteen centuries.

One caution, though. Not every good teacher holds an Ijazah yet. Some are still working toward theirs, and they may still teach your child well. Treat Ijazah as the gold standard, not as the only thing that counts.

How to Prepare for Ijazah Online

Years ago, you had to live near a scholar to do this work. That is no longer true, and the usual online path is clear enough. Start with a strong Tajweed foundation, so your recitation is ready. Pick your teacher with care. Does he truly hold Ijazah? Can he show you his Sanad? Which reading does he certify in? Most often, that will be Hafs from Asim. Then study one to one, several times a week. Ijazah preparation lives or dies on personal correction, and only private lessons give you that. Work through the Quran with your teacher, part by part, until every part is clean. When you are ready, your teacher issues the written Ijazah, Sanad included.

Online lessons fit this pattern surprisingly well. You get a private session, full attention on your recitation, and a timetable you can actually keep. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari 5027)

At Noor E Quran Institute, Ijazah preparation runs on that same one to one basis. The founder, M Muddasir Hameed, teaches every lesson himself, in a private setting that respects Islamic etiquette for sisters and brothers alike. A free 3-day trial lets you try the lessons first, and the monthly fee depends on how many classes you take each week, so you can build a steady routine before taking on a commitment that lasts years.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Ijazah in simple terms?

It is a scholar's written permission to teach the Quran. You receive it after reciting the entire Quran to a qualified teacher accurately, proving you have mastered it and may pass it on.

How long does it take to earn an Ijazah, and what does preparation cost?

Most students who already recite well and study several times a week need one to three years, because the whole Quran must be heard by the teacher. At Noor E Quran Institute, preparation lessons are charged monthly, and the fee depends on your classes per week.

Who teaches Ijazah preparation at Noor E Quran Institute, and can sisters learn privately?

The founder, M Muddasir Hameed, teaches every lesson himself, one to one. Sisters study in a private lesson, on their own, in a setting that respects Islamic etiquette, with no group class involved.

Can I prepare for Ijazah online, and does the free trial apply?

Yes, live one to one video lessons work well for this, since you recite the full Quran to your teacher over time just as you would face to face. A free 3-day trial is available, so you can try the lessons before committing.

title: Nazra vs Hifz vs Tajweed: Which Quran Course Is Right?
metaDescription: Not sure which Quran courses online fit your child or you? Compare Nazra reading, Hifz memorization, and Tajweed recitation to find the right course today.
author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
"My son can read a little, but should he memorize now, or fix his pronunciation first?" A mother asked me that in a trial lesson last month, and honestly, it is the question behind this whole article. The answer is simple once you see the three courses clearly. Nazra is reading the Quran fluently from the book. Hifz is memorizing it by heart. Tajweed is reading it correctly and beautifully. Start with reading, polish it with Tajweed, and save Hifz for when reading is solid.

Parents get confused for a good reason. Every academy lists the same three names, and they sound like three levels of one course. They are not levels. They are three skills, and they feed into each other in a particular order. Get the order right, and your child moves forward without frustration. Get it wrong, and even a keen child can start to dread lessons.

Nazra: Learning to Read Fluently

The word Nazra, also written Nazira, means reading by looking. Your child sits with the mushaf, the printed Quran, and reads. Not from memory. From the page. The work is recognition, flow, and confidence, until a whole page feels easy instead of exhausting.

After Noorani Qaida, this is the next step, and it matters more than parents sometimes realize. Qaida gives a child the letters and the joining rules. Nazra gives them the Quran itself, Surah Al-Fatihah through Surah An-Nas, read aloud with growing ease. I have watched children go from sounding out every word to reading a page in one sitting, and that shift changes how they feel about the Quran.

Who is Nazra for? Children from about five, once Qaida is done or nearly done. Adults who want to read on their own. New Muslims building their first reading habit. Anyone who wants to follow Taraweeh without getting lost. A typical Nazra course runs one to three years, depending on age and practice. The target is plain: open any mushaf and read it with confidence.

Hifz: Memorizing the Whole Quran

Hifz is a different job altogether. The student memorizes new verses daily, that is sabaq. Then revises the recent portion, sabqi. Then goes back over older portions, manzil, again and again, so the memorization holds. It takes three to five years, and it takes real daily commitment.

Here is what surprises parents. The new lesson is the smallest part of the day. A few lines, sometimes. Most of the time goes to revision. Huffaz will tell you the same thing, in their own way: keeping what you learned matters more than adding something new. Without that revision habit, memorization leaks away fast.

Hifz fits children around seven to twelve who already read well and can sit and focus, adults with a clear personal goal and a workable schedule, and any student who can give daily classes plus thirty to sixty minutes at home. If those pieces are not in place yet, waiting is not failure. Plenty of excellent Muslims read beautifully without memorizing the whole Quran. The question is not whether Hifz is noble. It is whether this student, right now, has the time, the motivation, and the support to carry it.

Tajweed: Reading It the Way It Was Revealed

Tajweed means to improve, to make something better. In practice, it is the rules of correct recitation: where each letter is pronounced from, the makharij, what qualities each letter carries, the sifaat, and rules like noon sakinah, meem sakinah, madd, and waqf. Dry names, I know. In a lesson, they are very alive. They are the difference between a letter that sounds almost right and one that sounds exactly right.

One misunderstanding comes up again and again, so let me clear it. Tajweed is not a stage you unlock after Nazra. It is quality, applied to whatever you read. A child picks up basic Tajweed during Nazra. A Hifz student needs it from the start, because a verse memorized wrong is a verse that has to be unlearned later, and unlearning is slow work.

Allah says in the Quran:

وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا

"And recite the Quran with measured and distinct recitation." (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4)

That verse is why we take pronunciation seriously. It is also why the Prophet, peace be upon him, praised the skilled reciter, saying such a person will be with the noble and obedient scribes, the angels (Sahih al-Bukhari 4937, Sahih Muslim 798). Tajweed is for anyone who reads at a basic level and wants to read better, for Hifz students, and for adults who learned to read as children and never got the rules explained.

How the Three Compare

Put side by side, the differences are easy to hold in mind. Nazra aims at fluent reading from the mushaf, takes one to three years, needs twenty to thirty minutes a day, and starts after Qaida, from about age five. Hifz aims at full memorization, takes three to five years, needs forty-five to ninety minutes a day, and starts after strong Nazra fluency, from about age seven. Tajweed aims at correct, beautiful recitation, takes six to eighteen months for the core rules with refinement after that, needs twenty to thirty minutes a day, and can start at any age once basic reading is there.

Notice what that comparison tells you. Tajweed is the only one of the three that overlaps with both the others. It belongs inside Nazra, and it belongs inside Hifz. That is why I teach it alongside reading and memorization, not as a distant third course.

The Order That Works: Qaida, Then Nazra, Then Tajweed, Then Hifz

Children, and most adults too, do best in this order. Qaida first, three to six months, learning the alphabet, joining, and harakat. Nazra second, one to three years, reading the whole Quran with growing fluency and basic Tajweed woven in. Tajweed third, six to eighteen months of deeper study, often during the later part of Nazra. Hifz last, three to five years, only after reading fluently with Tajweed.

Why so strict about the order? Because skipping steps has a cost you can see in class. A child pushed into Hifz before fluent reading fights two battles at once, new words and new memorization. A child who memorizes without Tajweed memorizes errors. Fixing those errors later takes longer than learning them right the first time.

Adults have a little more freedom. You can combine steps, for instance learning Tajweed while you finish Nazra, because an adult can usually focus longer in a session than a small child. New Muslims often do well starting with an adult Nazra course, Tajweed basics included, and building from there.

So Which Course Is Right for Your Family?

Young children, four to seven, should start with Qaida and then Nazra. That route has worked for generations, and a fluent young reader makes a much stronger memorizer later. Older children, eight to twelve, who already read fluently, have a choice: keep going with Nazra and Tajweed, or, if the interest and discipline are genuinely there, talk to me about Hifz readiness. I assess that in trial lessons, not from a form.

Teenagers and adults, start where you are. If you cannot read yet, Qaida and Nazra. If you read but mispronounce, a Tajweed course online can change your recitation in months. If you read well and feel drawn to memorization, Hifz is open at any age. New Muslims, learn to read first, and let the rest follow.

Sisters, a word about comfort. At Noor E Quran Institute, every lesson is private and one-on-one, at home, taught by me personally. A parent or guardian is welcome to sit in. The setting is familiar, the etiquette is respected, and questions go straight to me.

Can You Do More Than One at a Time?

Yes, and most students do. Tajweed pairs naturally with Nazra or Hifz, often as a focused class twice a week plus daily practice. The only pairing to avoid is starting Hifz before fluent reading. Apart from that, combining courses is normal, and often the fastest way to progress.

In short, start with fluent reading, refine it with Tajweed, and take up Hifz when the time is right. The best course is the one that fits where you or your child stand today, not the one that sounds most impressive.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which course should my child start with, Nazra, Hifz, or Tajweed?

Start with Nazra after Noorani Qaida, and add Tajweed basics as reading improves. Hifz comes later, only once reading is fluent. If you are unsure, book a free 3-day trial and I will assess your child's level and recommend the right starting point.

author: M Muddasir Hameed
content:
If you are a sister looking for a female Quran teacher online, I understand exactly why. Reciting aloud in front of a stranger is personal enough without worrying about hijab, the camera, or an awkward question. Let me explain what sisters usually gain from a female teacher, what to check before you choose one, and, honestly, what I can and cannot offer you here.

First, the honest part, because I would rather lose a booking than mislead you. At Noor E Quran Institute there is no female tutor waiting to be assigned to you. I am M Muddasir Hameed, the founder, and I teach every lesson myself, one student at a time. If a female teacher is a firm condition for you or your daughter, I will not pretend otherwise, and the checklist below will help you judge one properly wherever you find her. If you are open to a private lesson with me, the rest of this article explains how that works and why many sisters still choose it.

Why Comfort Changes How Fast a Sister Learns

Quran learning is not like watching a lecture. You recite, you get it wrong, you get corrected, and you try again. That only works when you feel safe enough to make mistakes out loud. A student who feels watched or judged will whisper, rush through verses, and ask nothing. A student who feels at ease will slow down, repeat a line ten times, and ask the question she actually needs answered.

For sisters, that safety is often tied to modesty. Reciting on camera, worrying about hijab, or asking about a ruling to do with menstruation can feel awkward with a male teacher. Nobody should have to push that feeling aside just to learn. Allah commands measured, careful recitation, and you cannot give a verse that care when your whole attention is on feeling uncomfortable:

وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا

"And recite the Quran with measured recitation." (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4)

That is the real reason online classes for women have grown so fast in London, Toronto, Sydney, and Dubai. A sister can learn from home, in her own space, at a time that fits school runs and work, instead of travelling to a class where she feels exposed.

What Sisters Usually Gain From a Female Teacher

1. Ease around modesty and personal questions

The most obvious gain is simple: no worrying about hijab on camera, no second guessing about camera angles, no hesitation before a personal question. Rulings about touching the Mushaf, making up missed prayers, or fitting practice around a baby all come up in real lessons. With a sister teacher, those questions tend to come out in the first week instead of sitting unasked for months.

2. Someone who understands a mother's week

A female teacher who is herself balancing children, housework, and worship will not be surprised when practice slips because a child was unwell. She adjusts the plan instead of scolding you for it. That understanding keeps mothers going after a bad week, where a rigid timetable would have made them quit.

3. A role model for young girls

For a young girl, the teacher is often the first person outside her family who shows her what a knowledgeable Muslim woman looks like. A Hafiza or an Alimah who recites beautifully and treats her kindly can shape a girl's confidence as much as her Tajweed. Parents often tell me their daughters open up faster, chat more, and actually look forward to class when they feel that warmth.

4. Private attention, not a crowd

None of this helps much in a big group. In a group, many women stay quiet rather than recite aloud or ask a basic question. One-on-one, the whole lesson follows one student: her level, her pace, her goals. The teacher hears every verse, corrects Tajweed on the spot, and notices when a student has gone quiet for a reason.

What to Check Before You Choose a Female Tutor Anywhere

A female teacher is not automatically a good teacher, so check the same things you would check for anyone. Ask whether she has memorized the Quran, whether she holds an Ijazah in recitation with Tajweed, and what formal Islamic study she has done in Quran, Hadith, Fiqh, and Arabic. Ask how long she has taught children online, not just adults, because a five year old on a video call is a different job from an adult student. And never enrol without a trial. A trial tells you more in thirty minutes than a website tells you in a month.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, put learning and teaching the Quran at the very top of good deeds, and that standard is worth holding any teacher to:

"The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027)

Knowledge, patience, and honesty matter more than a polished advert. If a tutor will not answer plain questions about her qualifications, or pushes you to pay before a trial, walk away.

How Lessons Work Here, Plainly Stated

Here, lessons are private and one-on-one, taught by me personally, in a setting that respects Islamic etiquette for sisters and young girls. Classes happen at home, on Zoom or Google Meet, and a parent or guardian may sit in on every lesson. Many mothers watch the first classes from the next room until their child settles in, and I am used to that. It causes no awkwardness at all.

Timings are flexible across time zones, which matters for families in the UK, USA, Canada, and Australia. You choose mornings, afternoons, or evenings, and rescheduling around Ramadan, travel, or a busy period is straightforward if you tell me in advance. Many mothers learn alongside their children, while the kids have their class, the mother has hers, so Quran learning becomes a family habit instead of one more burden.

Starting is simple. You begin with a free 3-day trial, three full lessons with no payment and no obligation. I listen to your recitation, assess your level, whether you are a complete beginner starting with Noorani Qaida or an advanced student refining Tajweed, and then we agree a plan at your pace: reading fluency, Tajweed, Hifz, or Islamic studies. Between classes there are small practice tasks, and parents get progress updates. Most students notice clearer pronunciation and more confident recitation within the first month, not because of any trick, but because someone is actually listening to every verse.
