title: The First 30 Days of Learning the Quran Online: What Parents Should Realistically Expect
metaDescription: What should the first 30 days of online Quran learning actually look like? A week-by-week guide for parents, from settling in and first letters to the week-three wobble and how to fairly judge the first month.
featuredImageAlt: A young child reading the Quran from a wooden rehal at home in soft morning light, with a parent sitting nearby encouragingly during an online lesson on a laptop
content:
The first 30 days of Quran learning will not turn your child into a fluent reader, and any teacher who promises otherwise is selling you something, not teaching your child. What those 30 days will do, if the teaching is right, is settle your child into a routine, teach them the first sounds properly, and show you whether this teacher and this timetable actually fit your family. That is a lot to achieve in a month, and it is the honest measure of a good start.

I teach every lesson myself, one child at a time, and I have watched this first month play out many times. The pattern is remarkably steady. The first week is about comfort, the second week brings the first visible progress, the third week usually brings the first wobble, and the fourth week is when you can fairly judge what you have bought. If you know that pattern in advance, you will not panic in week three, and you will not be fooled by a flashy first lesson either.

Week 1: settling in matters more than speed

In the first week, your child is learning two things at once: how an online lesson works, and what the Arabic letters sound like. The second part gets all the attention, but the first part decides whether the second part sticks. A child who is nervous about the video call, unsure when to speak, or sitting in a noisy room will not learn letters well, no matter how good the teacher is.

So expect the first lessons to feel slow. I spend time greeting your child by name, showing them how the lesson will run, and letting them read a little while I listen a lot. For a complete beginner, that first week usually covers a handful of letters from the Qaida, learned properly rather than rushed through. It is far better for your child to know five letters with the right sounds than to have "covered" twenty letters they cannot tell apart.

What you can do in week one is simple and it helps more than anything else. Keep the same quiet spot for every lesson, keep the book open before the call starts, and sit nearby for the first few lessons if your child is young. You do not need to teach, and you should not correct your child over the teacher. Your presence is enough. It tells your child this half hour matters, and it lets you see the teaching for yourself. Our guide to what to expect in a free trial Quran class explains what a first lesson should look like, so you can tell a careful start from a careless one.

There is also a verse worth keeping in mind from the very first lesson, because it sets the pace for everything that follows:

وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا

"And recite the Quran with measured recitation." (Surah Al-Muzzammil, 73:4)

Measured, not fast. That is the whole method of the first month in one line. A child who learns slowly and correctly in week one will overtake a child who was rushed through pages, because correct sounds do not need to be unlearned later.

Week 2: the first real progress appears

By the second week, most children stop being nervous and start being curious. They know when the lesson starts, they know what the teacher will ask first, and they begin to recognise letters without being told. This is also the week when practice between lessons starts to matter. A child who reads their small homework three or four times between lessons will move noticeably faster than a child who only opens the book during the lesson itself.

Homework in these early weeks should be tiny and exact. Read one page three times, or practise two letters until they sound right. If your child is given a whole chapter to "revise" in week two, that is not homework, it is guesswork, and it will put them off. Small homework done properly builds the habit that carries the whole Quran journey later.

You will also start to see what your child actually finds hard. Some children mix up similar letters for weeks. Some are shy readers who whisper. Some rush, and every word comes out in a hurry. None of this is a problem in week two. It is information, and a good teacher uses it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027) Learning is praised here before teaching, and it is praised without any condition about speed. Your child's slow, careful reading in week two is exactly the kind of learning that hadith honours.

For a fuller picture of how each lesson is structured, our minute-by-minute walkthrough of a 30-minute lesson shows what happens from the opening dua to the homework, so the second week holds no surprises for you either.

Week 3: the wobble almost every family hits

Week three is where many parents start to worry, and where a few give up too early. The novelty has worn off, the letters are getting a little harder, and your child may say they are bored, or tired, or that they do not want to go to the lesson today. This is normal, and it is not a sign that Quran learning is not for your child. It is a sign that the easy part is over and the real learning has begun.

The right response in week three is steady, not dramatic. Keep the lesson time fixed, keep the practice short, and talk to the teacher before you change anything. Often the fix is small: a lesson time that clashes with homework, a page that was too long, or a child who needs more encouragement and less correction for a few days. A teacher who knows your child will spot this quickly, because in a 1-on-1 lesson there is nowhere for a struggle to hide.

What does not help in week three is doubling the pressure. More pages, longer lessons, and scolding a reluctant child will make week four worse, not better. If the reluctance lasts beyond a couple of weeks, or if your child dreads every lesson, that is a different matter, and our guide to when a child loses interest in Quran class will help you tell a passing phase from a real problem with the teaching.

Week 4: how to fairly judge the first month

By the end of week four, you have enough to judge. Do not judge on fluency, because no child becomes fluent in a month. Judge on things you can actually see. Can your child recognise and sound out the letters they have learned, without guessing? Do they know what to practise, and can they tell you what they learned in the last lesson? Do they sit down for the lesson without a battle most days? Has one letter they always got wrong started to sound right?

If the answer to most of those is yes, the first month has worked, even if your child is still only on the Qaida. The Qaida stage is the foundation of everything that follows, and our guide to what comes after Noorani Qaida shows where that foundation leads, from Nazra reading to Tajweed and then to memorisation, so you can see the road ahead instead of wondering whether your child is behind.

Judge the teacher on the same honest scale. Did the same teacher teach every lesson? Did you hear, at least briefly, what your child learned and what to practise? Were mistakes corrected kindly, with the child given another try, rather than rushed past? A teacher who cannot tell you what your child learned in a month probably did not have a plan for that month.

How many lessons, and what should practice look like?

Most families start with three lessons a week, which is enough to build a habit without tiring a young child. Two lessons a week can work for an older child or a busy family, but progress will be slower, and the gap between lessons makes forgetting more likely. Five lessons a week suits a serious Hifz student, but it is more than most beginners need in their first month, and it can turn a new habit into a chore before it has had a chance to settle.

Between lessons, ten minutes of reading most days beats an hour once a week. Short, regular practice is what turns a letter learned in a lesson into a letter your child owns. Sit nearby when you can, praise the letters that sound right before you mention the ones that do not, and never turn practice into a test. Your child already has a teacher. What they need from you is encouragement and a calm routine. Our guide to how many classes per week your child needs covers the balance between age, level, and frequency in more detail.

For families juggling school runs, work, and different time zones, our guide to flexible class timings explains how evening and weekend slots can be arranged around your local time in the UK, USA, Canada, or Australia, which is often what makes the first month possible at all.

Three mistakes parents make in the first month

The first mistake is comparing your child with another child. One child reads a page in week two, another takes a month to settle, and both can end up strong readers. Children start from different places, especially when one has heard Arabic at home and another has not. Comparison only teaches your child that Quran learning is a race, and races are exactly what put children off.

The second mistake is sitting through every lesson and correcting from the side. It comes from a good place, but it confuses your child about who the teacher is, and it makes them nervous about making mistakes in front of two adults instead of one. Sit nearby for the first lessons, then step back gradually, and let the teacher do the teaching.

The third mistake is expecting visible results too fast and changing teachers at the first wobble. A new teacher in week three means your child starts the settling-in process all over again, with a stranger, and loses the teacher who already knows which letters they mix up. Change teachers when the teaching is genuinely wrong, not when the learning gets a little hard. Learning is supposed to get a little hard. That is how you know it is working.

What the first month should leave your child with

At the end of 30 days, a beginner should have a small set of letters they can read confidently, a routine they understand, a teacher they trust, and a feeling, even a small one, that they can do this. That feeling matters more than any page count, because it is what brings them back for month two, and month two is where the real momentum starts.

If that sounds like what you want for your child, the way to test it is simple. Our step-by-step enrolment guide walks you through signing up, and the free 3-day trial lets your child experience real lessons before you pay anything. Watch the first lessons yourself, judge them by the measures in this guide, and give the first month the full month. Your child deserves a fair start, and a fair start is a slow, careful, encouraging one.

title: 10 Questions to Ask Before You Hire an Online Quran Teacher
metaDescription: Before you pay for online Quran classes, ask these 10 questions: who really teaches, what the fee covers, how progress is tracked, and how safe and comfortable the lessons are for your family.
featuredImageAlt: A parent and child at home on a video call with an online Quran teacher, with an open Quran on a wooden rehal stand nearby
content:
The cheapest way to choose an online Quran teacher is to ask ten straight questions before you pay anything. If a teacher or an academy cannot answer them clearly, that silence is your answer, and it will have saved you months of frustration, wasted fees, and a child who has learned to dread lesson time.

Most parents do the opposite. They find a website, they like the look of the packages, they pay for a month, and only then do they discover that a different teacher shows up each week, that nobody can tell them what their child learned, or that the lesson time quietly clashes with school. All of that is avoidable. You are not buying a product off a shelf. You are trusting someone with your child's Quran education, and a good teacher will welcome careful questions, because careful parents make steady students.

I teach every lesson at Noor E Quran Institute myself, one student at a time, and the parents who ask the sharpest questions before enrolling are almost always the parents whose children settle fastest. They know what they bought, they know what to expect, and they know how to judge whether it is working. Here are the ten questions I would ask if I were hiring a teacher for my own child, and what a good answer sounds like for each one.

1. Who will actually teach my child, every lesson?

This is the first question for a reason. Many academies show you one impressive teacher on their website and then hand your child to whoever happens to be free that day. A child who has to reintroduce themselves every week, explain what page they are on, and adjust to a new teaching style will progress slowly, if at all.

A good answer names one teacher, and promises that the same teacher teaches every lesson. Ask it plainly: will my child have the same teacher next month as this month? If the answer is vague, or if you hear phrases like "our team" and "whichever teacher is available", keep looking. Your child deserves a teacher who knows which letters they mix up, which surahs they have finished, and what they were praised for last week. At Noor E Quran Institute, that teacher is me, M Muddasir Hameed, for every student, every lesson, with no rotating team and no substitute.

2. What are your qualifications, and can I hear you recite?

A Quran teacher's qualification is not a certificate on a wall. It is their own recitation, their knowledge of Tajweed, and their ability to teach a child, which is a different skill from reciting beautifully yourself. Still, you are entitled to ask about both.

A good answer tells you where the teacher studied, what they specialised in, and how long they have taught children online. Even better, a good teacher will let you hear them recite in the trial lesson, so you can judge the recitation yourself rather than trusting a claim on a page. My own background is in Islamic and Arabic studies, including a specialisation in Islamic jurisprudence, and I have spent years teaching children and adults one to one. But do not take any teacher's word for it. Listen to the recitation, watch how they correct a mistake, and notice whether the correction is patient and clear or rushed and sharp. That tells you more than any biography.

There is a verse that belongs at the start of any search for a teacher, because it reminds us what learning is for:

رَّبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا

"My Lord, increase me in knowledge." (Surah Ta-Ha, 20:114)

A teacher who keeps learning, and who treats your child's learning as an amanah, a trust, will answer questions about their own study honestly, not defensively.

3. Will the lessons be 1-on-1, or will my child share the teacher?

This changes everything about the lesson. In a group class, your child might read for five minutes out of thirty while the teacher divides attention between several children. In a 1-on-1 lesson, every minute is your child's, every mistake is heard, and every correction is for them alone.

Ask how many students are in the lesson at the same time, and whether your child will ever be asked to wait while others read. If the price looks low, a shared class is often the reason. For Quran learning, especially for a beginner or a young child, 1-on-1 teaching is worth paying for, because reading is a skill that is learned by reading aloud and being corrected, not by listening to other children read. Our comparison of 1-on-1 and group Quran classes walks through the trade-offs in more detail, so you can decide what suits your child and your budget.

4. How long is each lesson, and how many lessons per week do you recommend?

Thirty minutes is the standard for a child, and it is standard for a reason: it is long enough to learn and short enough to stay focused. Forty-five minutes or an hour can suit an older student or a serious Hifz student, but for a young beginner, a long lesson often ends in tiredness rather than learning.

A good answer does not just give you a number. It explains why that number suits your child's age and level, and it warns you against overloading a beginner. If a teacher pushes five long lessons a week on a seven year old who has never read Arabic, that is a sales answer, not a teaching answer. Most families start well on three lessons a week, and our guide to how many classes per week your child needs explains how age, level, and family routine should shape that choice.

5. What will my child learn first, and what is the plan after that?

A teacher without a plan will open a book and hope for the best. A teacher with a plan can tell you, in one minute, where your child starts and what comes next. For a complete beginner, the honest answer is usually Noorani Qaida first, then Nazra reading of the Quran, then Tajweed, and then memorisation for those who want it.

Ask for the road map, not just the first step. What happens when the Qaida is finished? How will you know my child is ready for the Quran itself? A teacher who can describe that path clearly has taught it many times before. A teacher who cannot is likely to improvise lesson by lesson, and your child will feel the difference. Our guide to what comes after Noorani Qaida shows the full path, so you can check any teacher's plan against it.

6. How will I know my child is progressing?

This is the question that separates a professional teacher from a casual one. "Your child is doing well" is not a progress report. You should expect to hear, regularly and briefly, what your child learned, what they still find hard, and what to practise before the next lesson.

Ask how often you will get an update, and what it will contain. Will the teacher tell you which page or lesson your child is on? Will they flag a problem early, or will you only hear about it months later? A teacher who teaches 1-on-1 has no excuse for not knowing your child's exact level, and a parent who hears a short update after lessons can support practice at home instead of guessing. If a teacher cannot describe how they track progress, assume progress is not being tracked.

7. What does the fee cover, and what happens if we miss a lesson?

Fees should be boring and clear: a monthly amount, a number of lessons, and a lesson length. Be suspicious of anything else. Ask what the fee covers, whether study material is included, and what happens when life gets in the way, because it will.

The two things that matter most are rescheduling and refunds. Can a missed lesson be made up, and how much notice do you need to give? Is there a notice period if you want to stop, or are you locked in for months? A fair policy is written down before you pay, not explained after you complain. Our guide to what online Quran classes fairly cost explains what different packages usually include, so you can spot an inflated price or a suspiciously cheap one.

8. Can we try before we pay, and can we stop if it does not work?

Never pay for a teacher your child has never met. A free trial is the only honest way to judge teaching, because a website cannot show you how a teacher speaks to a nervous child, how they correct a mistake, or whether your child actually enjoys the lesson.

Ask how long the trial lasts, whether it is a real lesson or a sales call, and whether you can sit nearby and watch. A trial that is really a demo, where your child barely reads, tells you nothing. A real trial lesson, with real teaching, tells you almost everything. Noor E Quran Institute offers a free 3-day trial of real lessons, and our guide to what to expect in a free trial Quran class explains how to judge one fairly, including what to watch for while your child is learning.

The second half of the question matters just as much: can you leave easily? A teacher who is confident in their teaching will not need a long lock-in or a penalty for leaving. If stopping feels difficult before you have even started, imagine how difficult it will feel later.

9. What time will lessons be in our time zone, and how flexible is that?

This is a practical question, and it ruins more enrolments than any teaching problem. A lesson at 4pm Pakistan time is 11am in London, 6am in New York, and 9pm in Sydney. The wrong time slot means a tired child, a rushed parent, or a lesson that clashes with school every single week.

Ask for the lesson time in your own local time, not the teacher's, and ask what happens when your schedule changes. Can the slot move for exams, holidays, or a change in work hours? Families in the UK, USA, Canada, and Australia live in very different time zones, and a teacher who serves all of them should be used to arranging lessons around your evening, not theirs. Our guide to flexible class timings explains how evening and weekend slots can be arranged around your local time.

10. How are lessons kept safe and comfortable, especially for sisters?

Your child will be on a video call with an adult, in your home, several times a week. You are right to ask how that is handled. A good answer covers the platform used, whether the lesson is private, whether a parent can sit nearby, and whether cameras can stay arranged in whatever way your family is comfortable with.

For sisters and teenage girls, this question matters even more, and the answer should be practical, not dismissive. A 1-on-1 lesson from home, with a parent nearby and no other students listening in, is the most private arrangement available, and many families choose private lessons for their daughters for exactly this reason. If a teacher brushes this question aside, or insists on arrangements your family is not comfortable with, that is a complete answer in itself: this is not your teacher.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: "Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim." (Sunan Ibn Majah, 224) That obligation sits on us as parents too. Choosing the teacher is part of it, not just paying the fee.

Answers that should worry you

Good answers are specific. Worrying answers are vague, rushed, or defensive. Walk away, or at least pause, if you hear any of these: a different teacher every week with no explanation; a promise that your child will finish the Quran in a set number of months; pressure to pay for six months upfront before any trial; no way for a parent to watch a lesson; no progress update beyond "doing well"; or a fee that changes depending on how hard you negotiate. None of these are teaching problems. They are honesty problems, and honesty problems do not improve after you pay.

Also be careful about judging a teacher on the first lesson alone. A flashy first lesson, full of praise and easy pages, can hide weak teaching, and a careful first lesson can look slow. Our minute-by-minute walkthrough of a 30-minute lesson shows what a real lesson looks like from the opening dua to the homework, so you can judge the trial by its substance, not its sparkle. And if you ever do need to leave a teacher later, our guide to changing your child's Quran teacher explains how to do it smoothly, without unsettling your child.

How to use these questions

You do not need to interrogate a teacher like an exam. Send the questions in a message before the trial, listen to the answers during it, and write down anything that was vague. Then compare two or three teachers on the same ten points. The comparison is usually decisive: one teacher will have clear answers, a named teacher, a real trial, and a fair policy, and the others will have gaps exactly where it matters.

If you would like to put these questions to me directly, the way to do it is simple. Ask all ten questions, watch the trial lessons yourself, and choose the teacher whose answers hold up. Your child's Quran journey deserves a careful start, and a careful start begins with asking.

title: How to Track Your Child's Quran Progress: Reports, Milestones and Honest Signs of Real Learning
metaDescription: Parents, here is how to track your child's Quran progress: the five measures that matter, what a good report looks like, and the warning signs to watch for.
featuredImageAlt: A parent and young child sitting together at home beside an open Quran on a wooden rehal, with a simple handwritten progress notebook nearby
content:
Your child has had Quran lessons for three months, and if someone asked you what exactly they have learned, you would struggle to answer. That gap is not your fault, and it is not a small thing. A parent who cannot see progress cannot support it, cannot spot a problem early, and ends up either worrying for no reason or trusting blindly for too long. Real Quran progress can be tracked, simply and honestly, and this guide shows you how.

Progress in Quran learning is not one number. It is not how many pages your child raced through, and it is not how confident they sound on a good day. It is a handful of things you can actually observe: which lesson they are on, how accurately they read it, how fluently they read it, what they still remember from last month, and whether they understand anything of what they read. If you can answer those five questions, you know where your child stands. If your teacher cannot answer them for you, that is a problem worth fixing, not a detail to overlook.

I teach every lesson at Noor E Quran Institute myself, one student at a time, so I know exactly where each student is, what they find hard, and what they were praised for last week. Parents do not need a complicated system to check that. They need a short, regular update, a few milestones to expect, and the confidence to ask a direct question when something feels unclear. That is what this guide gives you.

What progress really looks like

Start by forgetting the idea that faster means better. A child who reads ten pages carelessly has learned less than a child who reads two pages correctly, with the letters pronounced from their proper places and the short vowels in their right places. Quran reading is a skill of accuracy first and speed second. Speed comes on its own, once accuracy is settled, and it cannot be rushed without cost.

Real progress usually looks quiet. Your child reads a line they could not read last month without stopping at every letter. A letter they used to mix up, like the difference between similar sounds, now comes out right without thinking. They sit down for the lesson without the old reluctance, because the work feels possible rather than overwhelming. None of this photographs well, and none of it makes a dramatic story, but it is the only kind of progress that lasts.

There is a Quranic reminder that learning was never meant to arrive all at once. Allah says:

وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْلَا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ جُمْلَةً وَاحِدَةً ۚ كَذَٰلِكَ لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤَادَكَ ۖ وَرَتَّلْنَاهُ تَرْتِيلًا

"And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Quran not revealed to him all at once? Thus is it revealed, that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have rehearsed it to you in slow, well-arranged stages." (Surah Al-Furqan, 25:32)

That verse is a comfort for parents as much as for students. The Quran itself came down gradually, stage by stage, so that hearts could hold it firmly. Your child's learning will follow the same pattern: steady stages, not a single leap. Judge the stage your child is in, not the distance to the finish line.

The five things worth tracking

You do not need a spreadsheet, and you do not need to test your child yourself. You need these five measures, and you need your teacher to speak about them plainly.

1. Which lesson, page, or surah your child is on

This is the simplest measure, and the one parents most often go without. After a lesson, you should be able to say: my child is on this lesson of the Qaida, or this page of the Quran, or this surah for memorisation. If you cannot, ask. A 1-on-1 teacher has no reason not to know, and no reason not to tell you.

Keep your own short note, just one line a week: the date, the lesson, and one comment. After a month, that note tells a story no vague reassurance can match. You will see whether your child moved forward every week, stalled for a fortnight, or jumped ahead too quickly to hold the work.

2. Accuracy: how correctly they read

Accuracy means the letters come from their right places, the vowels are not guessed, and the basic Tajweed rules for their level are followed. For a beginner, accuracy means reading the letters and joined words correctly. For a Nazra student, it means reading a page with few uncorrected mistakes. For a Tajweed student, it means applying the rules they have learned, not just knowing their names.

Listen to your child read for two minutes, once a week, and notice one thing: are the mistakes fewer than last week, or are the same mistakes still there? A teacher should be able to name the one or two mistakes your child is currently working on. If every report is just "doing well", with no specific mistake named, the teaching may be kind but it is not precise.

3. Fluency and confidence

Fluency is not speed. It is reading without long pauses at every word, without dreading the next line, and without needing the teacher to carry them through. A fluent child still makes mistakes, but they recover, they keep going, and they enjoy reading aloud rather than fearing it.

Watch confidence as carefully as accuracy. A child who reads slowly but willingly is progressing. A child who reads quickly but anxiously, or who avoids reading in front of you altogether, may be memorising the sound of a page rather than learning to read it. That difference matters, and it is one a parent can spot at home better than anyone.

4. Retention: what they still remember

Learning that disappears in a week was never really learned. Retention is what separates a lesson that was taught from a lesson that was kept. For a Qaida or Nazra student, retention means last week's lesson still reads correctly this week. For a Hifz student, it means old memorised portions still come back without relearning them from scratch.

This is why revision is built into serious Quran teaching. A good teacher revisits old work regularly, rather than always pushing into new pages. If your child only ever moves forward and never revisits, ask how revision is handled, because a tower built without revision collapses quietly. Our guide to revising the Quran without forgetting it explains how Sabaq, Sabqi, and Manzil revision works for Hifz students, and the same principle, short daily revision of old work, helps every level. You can read it here: How to Revise the Quran Without Forgetting It.

5. Understanding and manners

The fifth measure is the one parents care about most once the reading is settled: does my child understand anything of what they read, and does the learning show in their manners? A child does not need to study Tafseer formally to benefit from a simple meaning, a short lesson from a verse, or the etiquettes of handling and reciting the Quran.

Ask your teacher, once in a while, what your child learned beyond the page: a meaning, a short dua, or a point of adab. A teacher who can answer that is teaching a child, not just drilling a reader. Our guide to helping your child understand the Quran, not just recite it, gives parents simple ways to build this at home: How to Help Your Child Understand the Quran.

What a good progress report should contain

You should not have to design the report yourself, but knowing what a good one looks like helps you recognise a weak one. A useful update, even a short one, covers four points.

First, where your child is now: the current lesson, page, or surah. Second, what improved since the last update: one concrete thing, like a letter now pronounced correctly or a page now read with fewer pauses. Third, what is still difficult: one or two named difficulties, not a general comment. Fourth, what to practise before the next lesson: one small, specific task, like five minutes of a named lesson, not "practise more".

That is the whole report. It takes a teacher two minutes to give, and it gives a parent everything needed to support the child at home. If you are only ever told "your child is doing well", you have been given encouragement, not information, and encouragement without information cannot guide a decision. Ask for the four points, politely and directly. A good teacher will be glad you asked.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: "The one who recites the Quran skillfully will be with the noble, righteous angels." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 4937; Sahih Muslim, 798) Skill in recitation is a journey, not a single achievement, and a progress report is simply a map of that journey, showing how far your child has travelled and what lies on the next stretch.

How often should you check progress

Checking too often creates pressure. Checking too rarely lets problems grow. A rhythm that works for most families looks like this.

After lessons, expect a very brief note or comment: what was covered, and what to practise. Not a formal report every time, just enough that you are never guessing. Once a month, expect a slightly fuller picture: the lessons covered that month, the main improvement, the main difficulty, and the plan for the next month. Once a term, or every three to four months, expect a proper review: where your child started, where they are now, whether the pace suits them, and whether the lesson frequency or level needs adjusting.

That monthly picture is the one that protects your investment. Many parents only discover a problem after six months, when a child has stalled or lost interest, and by then the fix is harder. A monthly check catches a stall in week five, when a small change, a slower pace, a different practice routine, or an honest conversation, can put it right. If your teacher offers no regular update at all, build the rhythm yourself: ask for a short monthly summary, and keep your own one-line weekly note.

The first month has its own signs, and they are different from later months. Settling in, first confidence, and the common week-three wobble are all normal, and they are covered in detail here: The First 30 Days of Learning the Quran Online. Judge month one by settling and effort, not by pages finished.

Milestones to expect at each stage

Milestones help, as long as they are treated as guides rather than deadlines. Every child moves at a different pace, and a milestone missed by a month is not a failure. Still, parents deserve to know what the stages look like.

In Noorani Qaida, expect your child to move from single letters to joined letters, then to words with short vowels, then to longer words and basic rules like Tanween and Shaddah. A beginner who practises a few times a week often completes the Qaida in a few months, though younger children and children with no Arabic background may take longer, and that is perfectly normal.

In Nazra, the reading stage, expect the pace to feel slower at first. The first Juz can take a while, because your child is learning to read real Quranic text rather than textbook exercises. After that, pages come more steadily. Fluency grows page by page, and the teacher should correct gently but consistently, so bad habits do not settle in.

In Tajweed, progress looks different again. Your child may read the same page more slowly for a while, because they are now applying rules they previously skipped. That slower reading is progress, not a setback. Expect them to learn rules in a sensible order, starting with the most common ones, and to apply each rule in reading before moving to the next.

In Hifz, milestones are measured in portions memorised and portions retained. A new lesson each day, a recent revision portion, and an older revision portion form the daily pattern. If only new memorisation is tracked and old portions are never tested, retention will quietly fail. Ask how all three are checked. Parents considering Hifz should also read the readiness signs, because starting too early creates more problems than starting late: Is My Child Ready for Hifz?

If your child has just finished the Qaida and you are wondering what comes next, the full roadmap through Nazra, Tajweed, and Hifz is here: After Noorani Qaida: What Comes Next.

Warning signs: progress that is not real

Not all forward movement is progress. Watch for these warning signs, and treat any one of them as a reason to ask questions, not a reason to panic.

The first sign is rushing. If your child moves to a new lesson every time, no matter how many mistakes they made, the pages are being covered, not learned. The second sign is memorised pages mistaken for reading. If your child can recite a page from memory but cannot read a new line from the same page, they have memorised a sound, not learned to read. Ask the teacher to test reading on an unseen line occasionally.

The third sign is praise without specifics. "Excellent, wonderful, doing great" every lesson, with no correction and no named next step, usually means the teacher is avoiding difficult conversations. Children need honest, kind correction far more than constant praise. The fourth sign is a child who never practises and never gets asked about it. Practice between lessons is where progress is made, and a teacher who never checks it is teaching only in the lesson, which is never enough.

The fifth sign is a parent who cannot get an answer. If you ask where your child is, what they find hard, or what to practise, and you receive only general reassurance, that is itself the answer. You are not being given information because, in many cases, it is not being tracked. That is a fair reason to consider a change, and our guide to changing teachers explains how to do it without unsettling your child: When to Change Your Child's Quran Teacher.

What to do when progress stalls

Every child stalls at some point. A stall is not a crisis, but ignoring it turns it into one. Start by naming the stall precisely. Is it accuracy, with the same mistakes returning? Is it fluency, with reading still halting after months? Is it motivation, with reluctance growing week by week? Is it retention, with old work forgotten? Each kind of stall has a different fix, and a vague worry cannot be fixed.

Next, talk to the teacher before changing anything big. Ask for their view, and listen for specifics. A good teacher will already know about the stall and will have a plan: slowing the pace, revisiting an earlier lesson, changing the practice routine, or adjusting the lesson length. If the teacher is surprised by a stall you have seen for weeks, the tracking itself needs fixing first.

Then check the simple causes before assuming a deeper problem. Is the lesson time too late, after a long school day? Is the lesson frequency too low for the goal, or too high for the child's age? Is practice at home happening at all, or only on lesson days? Our guides to lesson frequency and to the first signs of lost interest help parents separate a teaching problem from a routine problem: How Many Quran Classes Per Week Does Your Child Need? and When Your Child Loses Interest in Quran Class.

Finally, give any change a fair trial, usually a month, and measure it with the same five measures. If accuracy, fluency, or retention improves, the change worked. If nothing changes after a fair trial and an honest conversation, it is reasonable to look elsewhere. That is not disloyalty. It is parenting.

How parents can help without adding pressure

Parents often ask whether they should test their child, correct their mistakes, or sit through every lesson. The honest answer is: support, do not second-teach. Your job is to make practice regular, short, and calm, and to leave the correcting to the teacher, especially if you are not confident in your own recitation.

Listen to your child read for a few minutes, a few times a week, and praise effort and improvement rather than perfection. "You read that line much better than last week" helps far more than "you made three mistakes". Keep practice short for young children, ten to fifteen minutes of focused reading beats an hour of reluctant drilling. Keep the same time each day if you can, because routine does more for progress than occasional long sessions.

Sit nearby for lessons when your child is young, at least sometimes, so you hear what the teacher asks for and what your child finds hard. You do not need to intervene. Listening is enough, and it makes your weekly note, and your monthly question to the teacher, far more informed. And if you are ever unsure whether the teaching suits your child, a real trial lesson answers that better than any website. Noor E Quran Institute offers a free 3-day trial, and the enrolment steps are simple: How to Enrol Your Child in Online Quran Classes. You can also put your questions directly before enrolling, using this checklist: 10 Questions to Ask Before You Hire an Online Quran Teacher.

If you want to see what a lesson actually looks like from the inside, so you know what to watch for when you sit nearby, this walkthrough covers a full thirty minutes: Inside a 1-on-1 Quran Lesson.

A simple way to start this week

You do not need to overhaul anything to start tracking progress properly. This week, do three small things. First, ask your teacher one question after the next lesson: which lesson is my child on, and what is the one thing they should practise? Second, write that answer down, with the date, in a notebook or on your phone. Third, listen to your child read for two minutes, and note one thing that is better than last week.

Repeat that for a month, and you will have something no marketing page can give you: your own record of your child's Quran journey, in your own words, measured by reading, accuracy, and retention rather than by promises. That record will tell you whether to celebrate, whether to adjust, and whether to ask harder questions. It will also, over the years, become something precious in itself: proof of a journey that began letter by letter, and grew, by the grace of Allah, into a lifelong relationship with His Book.

title: How to Prepare Your Child for Their First Quran Class: A Parent's Checklist
metaDescription: A parent's checklist for your child's first Quran class: what the lesson looks like, what to prepare, what to say, and how to make them want to come back.
featuredImageAlt: A parent and young child at home preparing for their first online Quran lesson, with an open Quran on a wooden rehal and a laptop showing a teacher on screen
content:
Your child's first Quran class does not need to be perfect, and it does not need to be a test. It needs to be calm, short, and welcoming enough that your child wants to come back for the second lesson. That is the whole job of a first class, and if you prepare a few simple things in advance, you give your child the best chance of enjoying it.

Many parents worry about the wrong things before a first lesson. They worry that their child knows too little, reads too slowly, or will be embarrassed in front of a stranger. A good first lesson is designed for exactly that child. The teacher will start where your child is, not where you wish they were, and will spend more time listening and encouraging than correcting. Your preparation matters more than your child's starting level, because a relaxed child learns, and a nervous child closes up.

I teach every lesson at Noor E Quran Institute myself, one student at a time, so I see first lessons every week. The children who settle quickest are rarely the ones who already know the most. They are the ones whose parents prepared the space, explained what would happen in plain words, and then stepped back and let the lesson breathe. This guide is the checklist I wish every parent had before that first lesson.

What a first Quran class actually looks like

Forget the image of a formal examination. A first 1-on-1 lesson usually begins with a short, friendly conversation. The teacher asks your child's name, how old they are, and what they already know, even if the honest answer is nothing at all. Then there is a gentle check of the basics: can your child recognise the Arabic letters, read joined words, or read from the Quran already? That check is not a pass or fail. It simply tells the teacher where to start.

After that, the teacher will usually teach a small piece of new work, read it with your child, and let your child read it back. There will be praise for effort, correction that is kind and specific, and a short practice task for the days before the next lesson. The whole lesson is normally about 30 minutes, which is long enough to learn something real and short enough for a young child to stay focused.

If you want to picture the shape of a lesson before the first one, this walkthrough of a full thirty minutes will help: Inside a 1-on-1 Quran Lesson. And if you are still deciding whether to book at all, a free trial lesson answers that question far better than any article, as explained here: What to Expect in a Free Trial Quran Class.

The week before: a simple checklist

You do not need to buy anything special, and you do not need to teach your child anything in advance. Work through this short list in the days before the lesson, and you will remove almost every avoidable problem.

1. Fix the time, and protect it

Choose a time when your child is not tired, hungry, or rushing back from school. For most children, a lesson straight after a long school day is the hardest slot, while a lesson after a short break and a snack works much better. Tell the rest of the family the lesson time, so nobody walks in, calls your child away, or starts a noisy chore in the next room. A protected half hour teaches your child that Quran time matters in this house.

Families in the UK, USA, Canada, and Australia often juggle different time zones, and evening lessons after school are popular for exactly that reason. If you are still choosing a slot, our guide to timings for busy families may help: Flexible Quran Class Timings for Busy Families.

2. Set up a quiet corner, not a classroom

Your child needs a chair, a table, good light, and as little background noise as possible. That is all. A bedroom corner, a dining table after dinner, or a quiet living room corner all work well. Keep a glass of water nearby, and keep toys, television, and younger siblings' play out of sight for those thirty minutes if you can. The goal is calm, not ceremony, so do not turn the house upside down to create a perfect study. A familiar, comfortable spot beats an impressive one.

3. Check the device the day before, not five minutes before

Open the lesson link or app the day before, check the camera and microphone, and charge the device. Test the sound with your child, so they can hear and be heard clearly. If you use a laptop or tablet, place it so the teacher can see your child's face and their book at the same time, which usually means slightly to one side rather than directly in front of them. A two minute check the day before prevents the most common first lesson problem, which is ten minutes lost to technical trouble while a nervous child waits.

4. Have the right book ready

If your child is a beginner, they will usually start with Noorani Qaida, and the teacher will tell you which edition or version to use. If your child already reads, have a copy of the Quran ready, ideally the same print your child will use for practice. Put the book on a rehal or a small stand if you have one, so your child does not have to hold it and look at the screen at the same time. If you are unsure which book your child needs, ask the teacher before the lesson rather than buying several versions. That question is one of the sensible ones to ask before hiring a teacher, covered in this checklist: 10 Questions to Ask Before You Hire an Online Quran Teacher.

5. Teach wudu and adab as part of the preparation

A first lesson is a good moment to teach, gently, that we come to the Quran clean and with respect. Help your child make wudu before the lesson, and remind them to handle the Quran with clean hands and to sit respectfully while reading. Keep it light, not strict. A child who associates Quran time with calm respect, rather than with fear of doing something wrong, will keep that feeling for years. The manners of learning are part of the learning itself, and they grow naturally when parents model them without making a fuss.

What to tell your child, and what not to say

Children take their cue from their parents. If you sound excited and relaxed about the lesson, your child usually will be too. If you sound worried, or you keep warning them to behave and not make mistakes, they will arrive at the lesson already tense.

Keep your explanation short and honest. You might say something like this: you are going to meet a teacher on the computer, he will ask you what you already know, he will read with you, and he will help you learn to read the Quran step by step. That is all a young child needs to know. Do not promise that it will be easy, and do not say that the teacher will test them. The word test alone can turn a friendly lesson into a worry in a child's mind.

Do not coach your child in advance by drilling letters the night before. A tired, drilled child arrives already bored or stressed, and the teacher learns less about their real level. It is far better for the teacher to see your child's true starting point, even if that point is the very first letter. Starting honestly means the teaching fits your child from day one, instead of being built on a performance that cannot be repeated.

There is a beautiful reminder in the very first revelation about how learning begins. Allah says:

اِقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِيْ خَلَقَ

"Read in the name of your Lord who created." (Surah Al-Alaq, 96:1)

Learning the Quran begins with reading, in the name of Allah, one step at a time. It does not begin with perfection. Sharing that idea with your child, in your own words, sets the right expectation: we are here to learn, slowly and steadily, not to impress anyone.

During the lesson: sit nearby, but let the teacher teach

For younger children, sit nearby for the first lesson, close enough to hear and to help with the device if needed, but not so close that you become a second teacher. Let your child answer, even if the answer is wrong, and let the teacher correct them. Jumping in to correct your child yourself, however kindly meant, teaches them to look to you instead of the teacher, and it can embarrass them in front of a stranger.

For older children and teenagers, nearby is still wise for a first lesson, but a little distance is fine. Let them know you are in the next room and available, and check in afterwards rather than hovering. Teenagers value being trusted, and a first lesson handled with that trust often goes better than one watched over every minute.

If your child goes quiet, or seems shy, do not panic and do not apologise for them. Shyness in a first lesson is completely normal, especially with a new teacher on a screen. A good teacher will not force answers. They will wait, encourage, and try a different approach, perhaps starting with something your child already knows, so the lesson ends with a small success rather than a struggle. That small success is what brings a child back willingly next time.

Parents sometimes ask whether online lessons are safe and private for their children, and that is a fair question to settle before the first lesson. Our safety checklist covers cameras, supervision, and what to check in any online class: Is It Safe for My Child to Learn Quran Online?. At Noor E Quran Institute, lessons are 1-on-1 and private, with no other students listening in, which is one reason many families, including families with daughters, prefer this format.

After the lesson: praise the effort, not just the result

What you say in the ten minutes after the first lesson shapes how your child feels about the second one. Praise effort and courage, not just correct answers. Say that you are proud they tried, that they sat nicely, or that they read a letter they did not know yesterday. Avoid a detailed review of every mistake, and avoid asking, in a worried voice, whether they found it hard. Children remember the feeling of the lesson far longer than its content.

Ask your child one simple question, and really listen to the answer: did you enjoy it, and would you like to do it again? If the answer is yes, you have what you need. If the answer is unsure, ask what part they liked and what part felt difficult, without arguing with their answer. Then share that honestly with the teacher, so the next lesson can be adjusted. That conversation between parent and teacher is the real engine of progress in the early weeks.

Set up a short, regular practice routine from the very first week, even if it is only ten minutes a day of reading the lesson just covered. Practice does not need to be a battle. The same time each day, a calm reminder, and praise for sitting down at all will do more than a long, forced session once a week. The first month has its own rhythm, including a common wobble in the third week, and parents who know that rhythm worry less when it arrives. It is described in full here: The First 30 Days of Learning the Quran Online.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027) Your child is beginning something the Prophet praised in the highest terms, and your role in these early days is to protect that beginning: to make it regular, to make it calm, and to make it something your child associates with encouragement rather than pressure.

Common first lesson problems, and how to handle them

Most first lesson problems are small, and all of them have simple fixes.

If the technology fails, stay calm and treat it as an ordinary problem, not a disaster. Rejoin the lesson, or message the teacher to rearrange, and reassure your child that it happens to everyone. A child who sees a parent handle a technical problem calmly learns that problems are fixable, which is a useful lesson in itself.

If your child cries, refuses, or says they do not want to continue, do not force the full lesson and do not end in anger. A short, kind ending, with a promise to try again another day, preserves the relationship with Quran learning. Then ask yourself, and the teacher, what made it hard: was the time wrong, was your child tired, or was the level too high? Often the fix is a different time or a slower start, not a different child. If reluctance keeps growing over several weeks, rather than fading after the first few lessons, our guide to lost interest helps parents tell a routine problem from a teaching problem: When Your Child Loses Interest in Quran Class.

If your child already knows more than the teacher first assumed, or less, say so plainly after the lesson. Teachers can only adjust what they know about, and a level that is too easy bores a child just as surely as a level that is too hard frustrates them. A quick message after the first lesson, saying what your child found easy and what they found hard, helps the teacher set the right level for lesson two.

If you are unsure how often lessons should happen, do not guess in the first week. Start with what your family can sustain, usually two or three lessons a week for a beginner, and review after a month. The right frequency depends on your child's age, school load, and goals, and it is covered in detail here: How Many Quran Classes Per Week Does Your Child Need?.

Preparing by age: a few differences worth knowing

Young children, roughly aged four to seven, need the shortest preparation and the most patience. Keep the lesson time short, sit nearby, and expect fidgeting, questions, and wandering attention. That is normal at this age, not a sign of failure. A teacher experienced with young children will use repetition, praise, and short turns, and will end while your child is still willing, rather than pushing until they are exhausted.

Children aged eight to twelve usually settle fastest. They understand the idea of a lesson, they enjoy visible progress, and they respond well to a small routine, such as a sticker chart or a note of which lesson they completed. Give them a little responsibility, such as keeping their book ready and making wudu on their own, and praise them for it. That responsibility builds ownership of their learning.

Teenagers need a different conversation. Explain why the lessons matter, agree the time together rather than imposing it, and respect their privacy within the lesson. A teenager who has chosen the time and understands the purpose is far more likely to stay consistent than one who feels the lessons were forced on them. Many teenagers also benefit from knowing the path ahead, from Qaida to Nazra to Tajweed, so the work feels like progress toward a goal rather than an endless routine. That path is laid out here: After Noorani Qaida: What Comes Next.

A one page checklist for lesson day

On the morning of the first lesson, run through this list, and you will be ready.

  • Lesson time confirmed, and the family knows not to disturb you for thirty minutes.
  • Device charged, camera and microphone tested, lesson link open and working.
  • Quiet corner ready, with a chair, a table, good light, and a glass of water.
  • Qaida or Quran ready, on a stand if you have one, open at the right place if the teacher has told you.
  • Child has made wudu, is dressed comfortably, and has had a snack and a short break.
  • You have told your child, in simple words, what will happen, and that there is no test.
  • You will sit nearby, let the teacher lead, and praise your child's effort afterwards.
  • Practice time for tomorrow is already in mind, short, calm, and at the same time of day.

That is the whole preparation. Nothing on that list is expensive, complicated, or stressful, and together those small steps remove the friction that turns a good first lesson into a difficult one.

Starting well matters more than starting fast

Parents often ask me how quickly their child will progress, and my honest answer is always the same: a child who starts well, with a calm routine and a teacher they trust, will go further than a child who starts fast but dreads every lesson. The first lesson is not about how much your child learns in thirty minutes. It is about whether they leave thinking, I can do this, and I would like to try again.

Prepare the space, prepare your child with kind words, and then trust the process. Sit nearby, listen, and let the teacher do the teaching. Praise the effort afterwards, set up a short daily practice, and keep the routine steady for the first month. If you do those things, you have done your part, and the learning will follow, letter by letter, lesson by lesson, by the grace of Allah.

If you would like your child's first lesson to be a free trial, with no commitment and no payment, you can arrange it through the contact page. Trial lessons are available at times to suit families in the UK, USA, Canada, and Australia, and the enrolment steps are simple: How to Enrol Your Child in Online Quran Classes. A calm first lesson is the best way to find out whether a teacher is right for your child, and there is no better preparation than simply beginning.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much do online Quran classes cost?

Fees depend on the course and the number of lessons per week, so a beginner Qaida package costs less than a daily Hifz package. You can see the current packages on the website, and the free 3-day trial lets you confirm the value before you pay anything.

Do you offer a free trial before we commit?

Yes. Noor E Quran Institute offers a free 3-day trial, so your child can experience real lessons and you can check whether the teaching style and the time slot suit your family before you pay anything.

Who teaches the classes at Noor E Quran Institute?

All classes are taught by the founder himself, M Muddasir Hameed. There is no rotating team and no substitute teacher, so your child learns from one teacher who knows their level, their strengths, and what they found hard in their first lesson.

Are private lessons comfortable for sisters and teenage girls?

Yes. A 1-on-1 lesson means no other students listening in, lessons from home with a parent nearby, and a timetable your family controls. Many families choose private lessons for their daughters precisely for this privacy and comfort.

title: Quran Classes for Siblings: How to Arrange Lessons for Two or More Children
metaDescription: How to arrange Quran classes for siblings: back-to-back private lessons, different levels, family pricing, time zones, and a routine the whole family can keep.
featuredImageAlt: Two young siblings sitting side by side at home during an online Quran lesson, with an open Quran on a wooden rehal and a laptop on the table
content:
If you have two or three children and you want them all to learn the Quran, the simplest arrangement is also the most practical one: each child gets their own short, private lesson, one after the other, with the same teacher. That way nobody waits around, nobody gets compared in the middle of a lesson, and the whole family routine fits into one tidy block of the evening.

This is how most families at Noor E Quran Institute arrange it. The children sit down at their set time, the elder one takes the first lesson while the younger one finishes homework or plays quietly nearby, and then they swap. Parents tell me it turns Quran time into a family habit rather than a daily negotiation, and that is half the battle won.

Why Siblings Do Better With Their Own Lesson Each

It is tempting to put two children in front of the screen together and call it one lesson. It feels cheaper and simpler. In practice, it rarely works well, because two children are almost never at the same level. One reads fluently while the other is still sounding out letters, so one of them is either bored or lost for most of the session.

A private lesson solves that problem completely. Each child works at their own pace, on their own lesson, with the teacher's full attention for the whole session. The younger child is never rushed to keep up with an older brother or sister, and the older child is never held back. They still share the routine, the teacher and the excitement, but the learning itself stays personal.

There is a second benefit parents often mention: children behave better when the lesson is theirs alone. A child who might show off or go quiet in front of a sibling usually speaks up freely in a private session. The teacher can hear every letter clearly, correct mistakes straight away, and build a real relationship with each child as an individual.

How Back-to-Back Lessons Work in Practice

The usual pattern is simple. You pick a block of time that suits your family, for example 5:00 to 6:00 in the evening, and the lessons run back to back inside it. A family with two children might take 30 minutes each. A family with three children might take 25 minutes each, or a mix of lengths depending on age.

Between lessons there is a short changeover while one child finishes and the next one settles in. The teacher already knows both children, both levels and both lesson plans, so nothing is lost in the handover. Homework for each child is set separately, and progress is tracked separately too.

This arrangement also keeps the evenings manageable. Instead of Quran lessons scattered across the day, the family has one Quran hour, and once it is done, it is done. Parents in the UK, USA, Canada and Australia tell me this is the part they value most, because it fits around school runs, work and dinner without taking over the whole evening.

Different Ages, Different Plans

A seven-year-old starting Noorani Qaida and a twelve-year-old working on memorisation need completely different lessons, and that is fine. The teacher plans each child's lessons separately, even though the sessions sit side by side in the timetable.

The younger child might spend their lesson on letter recognition, joining letters and short words, with plenty of repetition and encouragement. The older child might spend theirs on a new memorisation portion, revision of yesterday's lesson, and recitation with Tajweed correction. Neither child is asked to do the other's work, and neither feels that Quran learning is a race.

Over time, the younger child often starts to look forward to "their turn" because they have seen their older sibling do it every day. That quiet example matters more than any lecture about the importance of the Quran. Children copy what they see at home, and a house where Quran lessons happen every evening teaches its own lesson.

What About the Cost for Two or Three Children?

This is the question every parent asks, and rightly so. Enrolling more than one child should not mean paying the same full arrangement twice over without any thought for the family budget. At Noor E Quran Institute the monthly fee is kept affordable, and families enrolling two or more children can ask about a family arrangement when they get in touch. The exact plan depends on how many children you have and how many lessons each one takes per week, so it is worked out with you rather than guessed at here.

What I would say to any parent is this: do not let cost be the reason one child learns and another waits. Talk to the teacher first, try the free trial lessons, and agree on a plan that the family can keep up month after month. A smaller plan kept consistently beats a big plan that stops after three weeks.

For a full breakdown of how pricing usually works, read How Much Do Online Quran Classes Cost? A Parent's Guide to Fair Pricing.

Avoiding Comparison Between Brothers and Sisters

Every parent of more than one child knows the trap: "Your sister could read this when she was your age." It is said with love, but it rarely helps. Children who feel compared often stop trying, because trying and still being behind feels worse than not trying at all.

Private lessons protect against this in a natural way. Each child's progress is measured against their own last lesson, not against a sibling. The teacher praises each child for their own improvement, whether that is reading a new page, memorising five new lines, or simply sitting still and focused for the whole session.

At home, the same rule helps. Celebrate each child's own milestones. When the younger one finishes Noorani Qaida, mark it the way you marked the older one's achievement. When the older one completes a Juz, let the younger ones share in the happiness without feeling small. A house where every child's progress is celebrated is a house where children want to keep learning.

A Sample Week for a Two-Child Family

To make this concrete, here is what a typical week looks like for a family with two children taking lessons five days a week:

  • Monday to Friday, 5:00 to 5:30: the elder child's lesson, covering new memorisation, revision and recitation.
  • Monday to Friday, 5:30 to 6:00: the younger child's lesson, covering Qaida or Nazra reading at their own pace.
  • Between lessons: a few minutes for the changeover, a drink of water, and a quick word from the teacher to the parent if needed.
  • Weekend: light revision at home, no new lesson unless the family wants one, so the weekend stays relaxed.

Families who need fewer days can take three lessons a week instead of five. The pattern stays the same, only the number of days changes. If you are unsure how many lessons your children need, read How Many Quran Classes Per Week Does Your Child Need? before you decide.

Fitting Lessons Around School and Time Zones

Families abroad live in different time zones, and school hours differ too. A family in London, a family in Toronto and a family in Sydney will all need different slots, and the timetable has to bend around that. Lessons are therefore booked at a fixed time that suits your time zone, and that time stays yours week after week so children can build a habit around it.

Evening and weekend slots fill up first, because that is when most children are free. If your evenings are crowded, a weekend morning slot or a slot just after school can work just as well. The key is consistency: the same time, the same days, every week. Children settle into a routine far faster than adults expect, and once Quran time has its own slot, it stops being something you have to remember and becomes something that simply happens.

For more on finding a slot that fits a busy household, see Flexible Quran Class Timings for Busy Families.

Privacy and Comfort for Sisters

Parents sometimes ask whether their daughters will be comfortable learning with a male teacher online. The answer is built into how the lessons work: every lesson is private, one to one, with no other students present. Sisters learn in their own separate session, from their own home, with a parent nearby if the family wishes.

Many families choose to keep the camera off for their daughters, and that is fully respected. Learning the Quran does not require being seen; it requires being heard, and recitation is heard perfectly well either way. What matters is that your daughter feels safe and comfortable, because a child who feels comfortable learns far better than a child who feels watched.

Starting With a Free Trial for Each Child

Before you commit to anything, each child can try a free 3-day trial. This matters more with siblings than with one child, because you get to see how each child responds individually. One child might take to it straight away, while another might need a gentler start, and the trial shows you both reactions before you spend anything.

During the trial, watch for simple things. Does your child sit willingly? Do they answer the teacher? Do they come back the next day without being pushed? Those small signs tell you more than any brochure. For a fuller picture of what the trial involves, read What to Expect in a Free Trial Quran Class.

If you are ready to begin, the enrolment steps are straightforward, and they are explained in How to Enrol Your Child in Online Quran Classes. And if your children have never had a lesson before, How to Prepare Your Child for Their First Quran Class will help you get the first week right.

When One Child Is Away or Falls Behind

Life with children is never perfectly tidy. One child falls ill, another goes to stay with grandparents, and suddenly the neat back-to-back routine has a gap in it. That is not a problem. Lessons for the other children carry on as normal, and the absent child's lessons simply pause and resume when they are back. There is no need to "catch up" by doubling lessons the following week, which usually just tires the child out.

The same calm approach applies when one child progresses more slowly than a sibling. Children develop at different speeds, and reading is no exception. A child who takes longer over Qaida is not behind; they are learning thoroughly, and thorough foundations make fluent reading far easier later. The teacher adjusts the pace for each child quietly, without announcements or comparisons, and parents can help by doing the same at home.

A small shared habit helps here too: five minutes after lessons, when both children are together, each one reads or recites something small they learned that day. The younger one might read a few letters, the older one a few lines. It is not a test and nobody corrects anyone except the teacher. It simply lets Quran learning feel like something the family does together, even though each child's lesson is their own.

What the Quran Says About Teaching Your Family

Allah commands parents to take responsibility for their family's learning in clear words:

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا

"O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones." (Surah At-Tahrim, 66:6)

Scholars explain that protecting your family includes teaching them what Allah has revealed. When you arrange Quran lessons for all your children, not just the eldest or the keenest, you are acting on this verse in the most practical way possible.

The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said: "The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it." (Sahih al-Bukhari, 5027) A home where several children are learning the Quran together, each at their own level, is a home where this hadith is alive every evening.

A Final Word for Parents

You do not need to have it all figured out before you start. You need a teacher who knows each of your children by name and by level, a time slot the family can keep, and a routine that survives busy weeks. The rest grows on its own: the younger child watching the older one, the older one helping the younger one revise, and the quiet pride of a house where the Quran is read every day.

Start with the trial, one child at a time, and see how it feels. If it works for your family, you will know within the first week, because the children will remind you when lesson time comes. That is the surest sign of all.

If you would like to arrange lessons for your children, get in touch through the contact page and mention how many children you have and what time zone you are in. We will find a slot that fits the whole family.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much do Quran classes cost for two or more children?

The monthly fee is kept affordable, and families enrolling two or more children can ask about a family arrangement when they get in touch. The plan depends on the number of children and lessons per week, so it is agreed with you directly.

Does each child get a free 3-day trial?

Yes, every child gets their own free 3-day trial, so you can see how each child responds individually before committing to regular lessons for the family.

Who teaches the lessons?

All lessons are taught by the founder himself, M Muddasir Hameed, in private one-to-one sessions. Your children share the same teacher and the same family timetable, but each child has their own individual lesson.

Can my daughter learn comfortably and privately?

Yes, every lesson is private with no other students present, and sisters can keep the camera off if the family prefers. Your daughter learns from home, with a parent nearby if you wish.
